Self-cienialls the best riches. A young man idle, an old man needy. Bacchus has drowned more than Neptune. Better to slip with the foot than the tongue. A sharp reproof is better than smooth deceit. Gentility without ability is worse than plain beggary. g,he divinity that ends our shapes is the modern tailor. Teacher: "What regulates the supply 61 liquor in Maine?" Bright boy (who reads the newspapers) : "The demand." As sins proceed they ever multiply, and like figures in arithmetic, the last stands for more than all that went before it. " That politician is a rascal, and I'm going to tell himl so to his face." "You'll have to go on both sides of him, then." "There, now, isn't that a shame?" "What's the matter?" "Why, I've forgotten to attend my class in memory culture! In China all wines are drunk hot. The thrifty China- man believes that heated wine intoxicates more expedi- tiously than cold wine. • Young lady: "'And di you come down the same way you go up, Mr. Sandbag ?" Balloonist: "No, miss; I try to come down feet first." Sally Lunns are so called from Sally Lunn, a pastry cook of Bath, who used to cry them about in a basket at the close of the eighteenth century. A lady rider has had a saddle made Which will enable her to ride on the right or left side of the horse, as she chooses, but not on both sides at the same time. Envy is a wicked little ripple that distorts everything reflected in what should be the placid waters of the soul. And the smallest ponds are the most inveterate ripplers. "I wish you wouldn't look so lovingly at that Arab," remarked young Dolley to Miss Amy as they inspected the curiosities in the side show. "Why not?" asked Amy. "Because I don't like you to waste your sweet- ness on the desert heir." Was ever a comforting thought expressed more deli- cately than by a cheery girl, who said to one who was sad over the falling leaves, "Just think how much more room it gives you to see the beautiful blue sky beyond." True of other things besides leaves. A musician thus defines woman at various ages. At Sheen years she is an arpeggio; at twenty, she is an allegro vivace ; at thirty, she is an accord° forte; at forty, an andante; at fifty, commences the rondo finale; and at sixty, the tremolo alla sondina. According to the old myth, the Plicenix was said to live five hundred years, and then to retire to Arabia and there make a nest of spices, flap its wings so fast as to set fire to it, burn itself to ashes and then come forth a young bird once more, to live for another five centuries. lie: "My dear cousin, I assure you I would never rob those sweet lips of a kiss." Far from having any inten- tion of robbing you of a kiss, I was trying to give you one." • • Too Facreious.—Edith : "It's all over between Jack and me. Penelope." Penelope: "Why, what is the matter?" Edith: "When I said ' Good-morning 'to him yesterday, what do you think he asked me?" Penelope: "I am sure I don't know, dear." Edith: "He wanted to know if I had used somebody's soap—wasn't it dis- gusting? He tried to explain it away afterwards, but I told him he had said quite enough." POLITENESS DIDN'T Par.—A lecturer, who had for Several minutes harangued his audience on the beauties of politeness was interrupted by a man who arose and said—" That's all very well, cap—mighty fine talkin' an' all that, but in this town politeness don't pay." "You are mistaken, sir," the lecturer answered; "politeness pays in any and all towns." No you are wrong." the interrupter persisted; "it don't pay here. tell you why. For some time I have been eating at a lunch- counter round yonder, and I have noticed that every man sat up to the counter with his hat on, and as I wasn't brought up that way. I concluded to take off my hat, and I did so." "Well, but did anyone object ?" the lecturer asked. "Oh, no, there was no objection; but, you see, some fellow stole my hat." A Sahara SCROOLBOY.-1 certain lady in the suburbs of Berlin had sent her young hopeful to spend the after- noon with some friends in another part of the town. Of course, as it was a bit of a party the boy was dressed in his best. But at the time he should return home the rain came down in torrents, and Mamma was in terrible anxiety as to the arenehing I.er son would have; but telephones are plentiful and cabs are cheap in Berlin, so she telephoned to her friend to give the boy the sixpence for a cab (50 pfennig), and to her joy she was in time her friend soon answered back that she had got a cab and sent him off.'and in less than half an hour he came rushing up the stairs, but drenched to the skin and streaming with water. " But," cried Mamma, "they said you were sent in a cab. Did you not come in a cab ?" "Oh, yes, Ma. But when I ride with you, you always make me get inside; this time 1 rode on the box I." PLANTS ON WALLS.—SOMe Of your readers NM to be interested in growing plants on walls. I have found no difficuty whatever in having, net only wallflowers, but a considerable variety of flewering, plants on a brick wall! • which bounds my garden. Wallflowers sow themselves, and produce a succession of good plants, which appear not only on the top of the wall, but growing out of •crevices all the way up. At this moment we have in flower on the same wall, antirrhinums, cenotheras (even..- tog primroses), the somewhat rare White Mullein ( Tree,- baecuni lychnitis), and the little creeping mother o'thousands, besides miniature birch trees, goosebeiry bushes, and currant bushes. The wallflowers;! sowed pi the first instance, many years ago, merely lifting a bit . of MOSS from the top of the wall and scattering a few seeds ur.der it. From that time they have taken care of themselves, and are usually the first wallflowers to bloom in spring. The antirrhinums are of a specially good strain and rich colouring. I am sure that scores cf plants can be had to bloom on the top ot garden walla without the slightest trouble. The whole of the plants have named are self sown or probably the seeds have been dropped by birds.--.V.8.M. in Amateur Gardeniv, • Two ENTRIES ON THE Loo.—There are circumstances under which the most truthful and credible statements may be both misleading and unwelcome. During a cer- tain voyage of a down east vessel the mate, who asually ikept the log, became intoxicated one day, and was an- 'able to attend to his duty. As the man very rarely ~committed the offence, the captain excused him, and attended to the log himself, concluding with this : • " The mate has been drunk all day." Next day the mate was on deck and resumed his duties. Looking at the 'log, he discovered the entry the captain had made, and ventured to remonstrate with his superior. " Whaa was the need, sir," he asked, "of putting that down on the log?" " Wasn't it true ?" asked the captain. "Yes, sir; but it doesn't seem necessary to enter it on the log." " Well," said the captain, " since it was true it , had better stand—it had better stand." The next day the captain had occasion to look at the log, and at the end of the entry which the mate had made he found this item :—" The captain was sober all day." The captain summoned the mate and thundered. "What did you mean by putting down that entry? What was the need, I say? Am I not sober every day ?" "Yes.7sir ; but wasn't it true ?" "Why, of course, it was true." " Well, then, sir," said the mate, " since it was true, I think it 'had better stand—it had better stand." The mate then took his departure, dodging the marlinspike as he went. A GOOD RADICAL Nestm—A good old clergyman with an innate sense of humour used to tell a story of his own experience connected with the subject of baptism. It was about the year 1832, when the country population was greatly excited on the subject of the first Reform Bill. The village alehouse would be, naturally, the place where politics would be discussed, and, as is so inimi- tably described by George Eliot in "Felix Holt," the labourers would wax warm over their glass, as in these • days they do over the newspaper. They saw in the Re- form Bill the first glimpse of a possible though far- distant future for themselves, and hoped that: things were turning in the right direction, and all their thoughts - and interests centred in the news from London. A Dis- senter brought his child to the church for baptism /from the sort of feeling that evert wy ;-;:cvpi4 in son:lg rural dietricte tlaAt ctraml bsptisin preser ;§ -••• • •va qvil sarairso.l. . many eve. co which the flesh is heir. When -a -- the clergyman put the question, "Name this child," "Reform, sir," was the answer given. This was too much for the good old Tory parson, who said, "My good man there is no such name. I cannot give your child such a name. Cannot you think of another?" "Reform, sir !" was the answer, in more dogged tones than before; and it ended in the clergyman refusing to continue the service, the aggrieved father marching off in high dudgeon. The following Sunday found the father re- turned to the charge with the baby. The kindly parson, desirous of avoiding a repetition of an uncomfortable scene, went up to him and said, "You have thought of another name for your child, I dare say." "Yes, sir, was the more courteous reply; it's all right this time. Thus reassured, the clergyman began the service, and on saying the words "Name this child," the answer was "John Russell Brougham Feargus O'Connor," which string of names the crestfallen parson was obliged to give the poor infant, who, for aught I know, still lives to bear it. Whether they were all duly registered would be an amusing subject ot inquiry.—Cornhill Magazine.

"CAPITAL CHAT."
On Monday evening, the Prince of Wales dined with Lord Rlindolph Churchill in Conought-place. Among the guests invited to meet hi Royal High- . ness was Mr. Gladstone.

Mr. J. It. Dore, who has just discovered an un- known early addition of Tyndale's New Testament, which he has forwarded to the British Museum, is the author of a work entitled "Old Bibles," of which Messrs. Eyre and Spottiswoode are the publishers. The recently discovered work corresponds with Tyndale's Testament of 1334-5,

A somewhat serious misunderstanding has arisen in !connection with Mr. Plimsoll's Deck-Loading Bill. It bears on its back the name of Mr. Broad- hurst, who is strongly opposed to one of the princi- pal clauses in the Bill which prohibits the importa- tion of live cattle. Mr. Broadhurst has written to Mr. Plimsoll asking him to take steps to have his name removed from the Bill.

The Munich folk enjoy the distinction of being the greatest beer drinkers in the world. Roughly speaking, their consumption has been calculated to be about a quart and a half a day for every head of the population. London falls somewhat short of half that amount. Berlin is a trifle below London, and Vienna a trifle above. As all persons who have been in Germany know, the Munich beer is the most famous of all.

The Empress, after all, might have spared herself the trouble of going to Athens, as the accouchentent of the Duchess of Sparta is well. over three weeks before it was expected. The birth of a son to the heir of the throne will cause great delight in Greece, as there is an ancient tradition that whenever a son is born at Athens to a Royal couple named Constan- tine and Sophia, the Greeks will quickly recover possession of Constantinople.

Dr. Moulton, who was elected president of the Wesleyan Conference on Tuesday, is one of the most eminent exponents of Methodism. He was a mem- ber of the New Testament Revision Committee, and is an accomplished Greek scholar. Dr. Moulton became a Wesleyan minister in 1858, and is well known as the Principal of the Leys School at Cam- bridge. He is a brother of Mr. Fletcher Moulton. Q.C., who represented Clapham in the Liberal interest in 1885.

Mr. Chauncey Depew, known throughout the United States as the best after-dinner speaker of the day, being, as our readers will have observed, at present in London, has sent to the Prince of Wales a copy of a volume containing a collection of his recent public speeches. In ari autograph letter, the Prince acknowledges receipt of the book, plea- santly adding that a perusal of it will assist him in preparing the numerous addresses he is called upon to deliver on ceremonial occasions.

Mr. Stead has got Oliver Cromwell's pistol. It was presented to him by a friend, and be is very proud of it. Cromwell occupies a prominent place in Mr. Stead's gallery of heroes,and, after the Bible, Cromwell's letters and speeches had the greatest influence on him as a young man. The pistol is in good order, and would shoot a cavalier yet. Mr. Stead has hung it up on the walls of his sanctum on the Embankment, underneath an old and curious portrait of Cromwell—painted en a panel.

Revenge, according to Lord Bacon, is a kind of wild justice, and the ordering abroad of the Grena- dier Guards appears .to be something of the same kind. The whole battalion is, to be punished for u fault which rests from first to last with the officers. At the same time it must be admitted that the officers will feel it most. The curled darlings of London Society will be much more "oat of it" at Barbados, Cyprus, or the Cape, than even poor "Tommy." This is " a kind of justice," but it is a very wild kind.

The arrangements for Mr. Gladstone's next visit to Midlothian are rapidly bein"P.completed. It will take place at the end of October, and, as at present arranged, the oratorical efforts will be limited to the usual three great meetings at Edinburgh, Dalkeith, and West Calder. But representations, hear, are being made to the effect tha Mr. Gladstone, who will once more be the guest of Lord Itosehery, at Dalmeny, shall address a series of village-meetings, so that thoss electors who have come upon the register since-his last visit shall have an opportunity of becoming personally acquainted with, him; and it would not be surprising if these have-the desired result.

The stories about Prince Bismarck's memoirs and reminiscences are all nonsense. The' Empress Frederick has not only informed the Prince that she positively forbids him to pnblish any letters written by her or by her husband, but she has eaused the Emperor William to remind the ex-Chancellor of the general order which was promulgated after the trial of the late Count Arnim. This order, which was drafted by Prince Bismarck, arab approved by the old Emperor William, and also by the Emperor Frederick (then Crown Prince), provides that no German Minister is tnprint or publish any book, or pamphlet, or paper of any kind,. relating to State business, without the express permission of his Sovereign.

Lady Salisbury launched out into a ball on, Wed- nesday evening for the benefit of her remaining unmarried daughter, and Torydom mustered its social forces in great numbers. The staircase and gallery at the entrance of the Premier's house in Arlington-st., are always imposing features of his domestic entertainments, while the ball-room is an excellent one. The Prime Minister looked on, apparently much interested in the gyrations of his guests, hut did not show any inclination to dance. The fact is that his lordship is not a dancer, and not even the pleadings of princes have ever lured him even into a square. Lord Cranborne, however, is a great performer on the floor.

The mysterious gentleman who piped the rats of Hamelin into the Weser, has been paralleled in Australia. Everyone knows about the Australian rabbit plague. Well, Lord Hopetoun has just re- turned home from an extensive tour on horseback through the north-west of Victoria—a district that a few years ago was swarming with rabbits—and he reported to a meeting in Melbourne his surprise at ht Ting seen not more than a dozen rabbits during the Whole of his trip. At a later stage of his speech he mentioned how gratified he was, as a Scotchman, to find at a halting place in that remote region a Highland piper awaiting his arrival. "That accounts for the disappearance of the rabbits," somebody interjected.

"Our Naples skies," writes a correspondent, " are just now very beautiful, the weather being clear and serene. Golden and pearly dawns are succeeded by a heaven of marvellous blue, and this again by rosy sunsets and purple nights. The planet Jupiter is rising grandly in the east, his beams distinctly re- flected on the unruffled sea, while Venus is bril- liantly setting in the west, and red Mars is the first star seen high in the southern heaven when twi- light fades. During the pure cool nights, the different constellatiots pursue their solemn course with a splendour scarcely known-further north, and every vagrant shooting-star is visible in the transparent firmament,while now and then a green meteor glides slowly down from the zenith and seems to melt away in liquid drops."

The King of Siam is in Singapore, and has de- livered himself in that city of a jest. It is unfortu- nately somewhat in the vein of the dialogue of Messrs. Brander Matthews and Jessop's American play at the Gaiety, but it is the jest of a reigning monarch, and as such deserves, as Dr. Johnson says, to' be handsomely acknowledged." His Majesty was visiting a certain shop, where he was shown a knife by an assistant, who zealous for the interests of his emyloyers asked " a truly Royal price for it." Smiling as he turned the knife over in his hand the king is reported to have said," Well, I don't think this knife would kill anybody. but I am afraid its price would." "With this sharp thrust," says the historiographer of the "faits et gestes" of the Royal progress, " his Majesty passed on."
Mr. Howard Vincent wants to have the foreign- ers domiciled in England specially tabulated in the census. Certainly. There are two classes of

foreigners: in England. One class work for their living; the others don't. It must, of course, be the latter that Mr. Vincent, as a Protectionist, has got his eye on. There are the Leiningens, the Batten- bergs, for instance, and a horde of Germanparasites who do nothing but make a very respectable living on the natives. Mr. Vincent,as a logical Protection- ist, must object to the free importation of these Germans. He would put a duty on the food which we eat, on the goods which we use, and on machin- ery, which are instruments of production. The least , he can do, therefore, is to advocate a prohibitive duty on these princely Teutons who have fastened themselves upon us. We would suggest that the duty should in some way be made retrospective.

A correspondent writes:—" What a pity it was that our good ancestors who want us to pay not once, but a hundred times, their debts in pleasure, gambling, and folly, did not bethink themselves of the plan of making generations unborn/pay for some of the finer delights which they enjoyed? For in- stance, we have to compensate the descendants of Charles the Second's mistresses. But if there is to be this kind of heredity in badness, why not at least extend the principle to poets and thinkers, as well as courtiers and courtesans? Why has there not been an Earl Milton or a Marquis of Stratford— tapping the revenues to the tune of £5,000 a year, because in their veins,has flown some drops of the blood- to which we owe *Hamlet' or Paradise Lost?' Surely, the descendants of Shekespere, Mil- ton, and Dryden would have more claims on our consideration than the children of Nell Gwynne or Louise de Querouaille."

The Parentage of the late Sir Richard' Wallace was always hedged around with a good deal of mystery. The accepted story, of course, has been that he was a natural son of the Marquis of Hert- ford, the original of Tbackeray's Lord Steyne. The fact that Lord Hertford left him all his property has always given the strongest colour to this theory, but it is more than suspected that he did this as much out of a cynical desire to spite, the successor to the title as anything else. It may be mentioned that when the late baronet was born Lord Hertford was only a little over sixteen years of age, and among his friends and contemporaries it was always believed that Lord Hertford was not his father at all. Ms mother was a dancer, and she prevailed on Lord Hertford to undertake the care of Mr. Richard, as be was always styled, and be certainly was not reared or educated in the way that was best calcu- lated to equip him for the possession of the wealth of his reputed father.

Mr. Justice Kel-ewich's remarkable, grammatical ruling has brought us the following note from a correspondent :—" The Judge is said to,bave ruled that the correct possessive shape of the name Lewis is Lewis': This is quite new and unsound. The grammatical rum as to the omission of the posses- sive s' is really based on the exigencies. of phone- tics. That is, where the sibilant sound is repeated more than twice, which is as much as is convenient, the third sound is omitted, but the apostrophe left to indicate, to the eye only, the possessive case: Thus the omission only applies to the pluraposses— sive case, The-two Lewises's hat' is ehorteried, to ',the two Lewises" hat,' the double sibilartes being, enunciated, But in the singular possessive-the two sibilants are manageable by the voice—hence John Lewis's hat" is the correct form, which everyone uses. But to say that folks, instead of using this form, do and; should say Lewis' hat 'is bath bad in grammar and phonetics."
Man .Kelvot

CHAPTER VII, • 13LO,WN AWAY.. "Tice Court sentences him to suffer death by being blowes away from the muzzle of a cannon!" ' Such was the grim sentence now about to be carried into execution; and crowds of people, both Europeans and natives were hurrying into the parade-ground to see the ghastly spectacle. The man deserved his fate, no . doubt. In the circum- stances hislanguage and beating had been most in- jurious, and calculated to provoke mutiny already rearing its head. Their designs, had they been carried out, would have led to a wholesale mass:erre of the Europeans in the statical, and an examede must be made. Five o'clock was the hour named for the exeem- tion, and the sentence was ordered to be carried out in the presence of the tidope in the garrison. ,Before' that time all the men had been marched tip, and had occupied the positions assigned to: them, forming thremsides of a square, of which the: left and right were occupied by the native corps. Opposite these dusky soldiers was a: stern array of artillery, the gundloaded, and ready for action with the gunner standing by them; prepared, at the word of command, to fire on the Sepoys had they shown the least inclination to misbehave themselves or become unruly. The guns and gunners were of course of the Royal Artillery. Some English troops were also drawn up, and the gun f rom which the prisoner was to be Wown was placed facing the fourth side of the square, in front •of the open space. All, was silent. Not a mind was heard from the ranks as the treparations were made, land even the words of command were given in a ' subdued tone, as if for fear of disturbing -the sileuco. which had fallen upon the garrison. , It was curious to watch the faces of -those present, and had any of the spectators examined the coun- tenances of the Europeans and natives, he would have :distinguished a Vast differeneein expression. Ai mere ihandful of English soldiers of the line, with some 'eight or ten guns and artillerymen, were quite suffi- cient to keep in check the multitude of natives and the two strong Sepoy regiments, Fear and resolution were the two expressions peeeeptible—terror on tlic aide of the natives, and stern determination on the peat of the Europeans to punieh the offenders. An eye-witness of this impressive ceremony writes: " eemidst all the assembled thousands a murmur could not even be heard; a -whisper would almost have 'broken the stillness. The officers rode alone the lines resolved and silent. Somoiseless was th sr motion that even the champ of their horses' bits and the clank of their sabres jarred upon the ear." Five ceelock struck—slowly and with a • knelling sounelf— as the officer in command of the troOns, Colonel Deane, rode up in front of the guns. He looked wan and anxious, and no wonder. An aflec- ting interview had taken place-the day before be- tween him and Mrs. Layton, in which she had begged hard for her husband's life. But the commander could do nothing. The sentence had been confirm& Notwithstanding the aggressive circumstances and the provocation indirectly given, the assault had been committed suddenly. The priaoner had quitted the station without leave, had gone up to the hills, and. committed a most serious offence. There was . no- excuse in a military point of view, for the prisonex the colonel professed, as he felt, the greatest syme pathy, and endeavoured to console the yohng wife, excusing all her folly and vanity in her now real sorrow and anxiety. But he had 'declined to interfere, and she had called down upon him the vengeance of heaven, and sworn to be revenged if it cost her her life. Colonel. Deane was not a man to be frightened' at shadows, or intimidated by threats. But he was at ease; and when he understood that Mrs. Layton had secretly left the station with:the disgraced officer, his indignation was extreme. But he determined to, spare the feelings of the husband. No one was admitted to the cell in which the condemned man lay, and It. fortunately remained in ignorance of the circumstances. When the colonel bad taken his place in front of the gunsrhe commanded the sentence to be readlin Hindustath to the Sepoy, anddvehen this somewhat unnecessaredformality had been complied with, the man was ordered to prepares for the executiois.of the sentence; The stolid-looking native—a-fine man, with 'brio means unpreposessing featured—was stripped of his regimental jacket and, escorted by a guard of- the British regiment, marched up to the muzzle of the, gun. When he had reached it a smothered Eound was heard. It was the order to fix bayonets. The Enfield rifles were all loaded and at the shouldere At theleast signof insubordination the "Ready,Present, Fire" would have followed, and the native infantry would luweebeen annihilated under an enfilading fire. The emanonwere also maddready,and they:7.l,min muzzles, waiting only the teach of the port-fire to belch forth-their full contents upon the Sepoys,.had a most intimidating effects All round the parade ground were artillerymen' standing by ,the old guns upon the ramparts ready for action. leleanwblie the prison.er had been securely , strapped to the guneandefter a pause, the, clew steady vele* of the officer commanding the artillery ordering all to retire -from the gun excepting the gunner, who was standing with lighted pert-fire ready to. discharge the cannon. "Ready," cried the officer. The peed-fire gleamedias it was blown, by the gunnodend the prisoner -shuddered visibly as the fatal moment approached: Ile had now only a few seconds to live. " nee t" exclaimed- thee captain. A roar, like an earthonalee„ appearing all the more loud from the oppressive -silence that had hung around; the parade-gxonad. A cloud ofdamoke wee slowlyedispersed. Some fragments of' something red were perceived failing. All was over: Without any del:valence natives hueried 'forward and picked or swept up these red fraghsents of what ten seconds before had' been a living, breathing mane in the full enjoyment of health- and strength., All was indeed ended foseshiza. The sun was already nearince the horizon, and ne time, was lost The other enisonere who had been, din'aerbed by the roar of the cannonehad now to, be ex:seated, and the guard was sent forhira. A firing party was told offend took up theiet positionseoppo- site tho wall by the bastion. There was a pause while the peoranan, pitied: by all; was beine fetched from his cell; but MI last he came forward—his face covered up in a cloth. Ile had himself wrapped his harelkerchief around before the gees/ached entered the eelL He did notavieh to be recoßised evidently,dee Ito had shave& his beard and had doffed): his unid ;form. He came forth with a. firm step, his. Oak 'shirt and a leairdef trousers with: boots being.hiceonly elothing. . The colcaell turned away; he could not heart* look upon them man whom ha. had endeavoureal to " save. Be pitied him from the bottom af his heart, but he vase powerless to alter the demn alrallaY pronounced. The prisoner walked firmly to the,spotted by a sergdant of the regiment by the sleewee and plena against the wall. He ;stood upriakt and) never flinched, nor did he speak, a 'word. His sentence was read to him, hat he made no '. observation, nor did ha take any- notice of the chaplain beside him. Idany remaelted haw wasted ehe hariebeeoree, and in defiance of discipline several j` men. of the regiment alaisperedt that they would scarcely have recognised him as the same- man. The condemned man made no sign. The chaplain svhisperea to him that all was ready, awl offered up a prayer by the prisoner's special request. Layton's lies. moved in reply to the Amen; but no sound eseaped his lips. Then the clergyman withdrew,. wondering that his services had been declined all tile day before, and requested at the last. 'Ready!" cried the colotheL The Enfields clattered and rattled. A twitching; of the hands, a. tight compretsion of the fists, was the only evidence that the sergeant had heaxd: the order.

----• " Present—fire!" The volley rang out. The aim was true and steady. We suffering—no pain. Scarce had ths owcis left the officer's lips when the prisoner dropped lifeless upon the parade! Many a hardened soldier gulped down the strange rising lump in his throat as he "recovered" his arms. Many an " old hand" passed Isis fingers eau. tiously to his eyes, and some men even turned away unreprimanded. AP Then a fatigue party came forward, and as the glorious sun dipped into a golden sea the guns were limbered up, and the troops were marched from the parade. The crowd gradually dispersed, and the bearers lifted the body of their late comrade. "Better take off this handkerchief," they said. "Can't bury the poor chap like this." "He died like a man," remarked another, huskily. "and without a wad.. Come Qu,"

They were about to raise the body when the Corporal in charge reverently removed. the handker- chief from the face of the corpse. It was blood- stained and tightly tied. He had some difficultyto loose it. .

Curious fancy," he murmured. "Poor chap! Why, God alive, who's this ? " he exclaimed, in horror. The men laid the body hastily down, and gazed Into the dead man's face, horror stricken. The features of the corpse were now fully dis. closed—the staring eyes open to the sky—the features rigid. "Mr. Soutar, by all that's good!" Yes there *as no doubt about it; it was indeed the unhappy young officer who had changed places with the man he had injured, and life having no charms for him, had suffered for the husband of the woman he had once sought to ruin, and who had forgiven him. Let us hope that the God he had so often offended lied forgiven him too.

Had not everyone been so occupied in witnessing the execution many of the spectators might have perceived a man disguised as a native hastening across the cantonment in the direction of the river. He proceeded rapidly and yet with caution. In five minutes he had disappeared, and sergeant Layton was' dead to home, and wife, and comrades. His place knew him no more, nor would he ever again be seen till he had retrieved his am and fame.
His wife, intent on schemes of vengeance, a de- ceived and reckless woman had left the station, and was about to embark for England, bellowing he was dead.
But they were fated to meet again.

This time they had only a single horseman to deal with, and in answer to their questions get forreply— " Sower," which means horse-soldier or trooper. Colonel Deane's inquizies for the mysterious indi- vidual who had warned them failed to elicit any reply. Captain Hodson, whose name became sube- quently so celebrated, asserted that none of his men had been in the direction indicated, so far as he was aware. He had sent out his scouts, but none an- swered to:the description,; and the colonel was com- pletely puzzled. "Well, Hodson," he said, when he had procured from his friend some necessary articles of clothing, "this seems to me to•be a serious businessb What will be the next step, do you think?" The smallness of the force, the constant reinforcement of the enemy, the want of. train and ' requisites. for an investment, all pointed to the necessity ,for a coup de main.. Certainly "Take Delhi.' This was the watchWordeso te,speak. So the orders were issued and the men marched silently down, the 60th .Rifles well to tbelnont, 8: usual. Silently the columns advanced intha darkness. Sir J. FERGUSSON, in reply to Mr. S. Leighton, said there was no intention on the part of the Government to concede to the French the right to occupy Zeila.. Mr. Balfour intimated that next day he would read a com- munication from Judge Harrison lan the remaspos he recently made in a charge to the grand jury, which were construed as an incitement to the people of Galway to resort to lynch law. Mr. MATTHEWS, in reply to Mr. Cunninghame Graham, said the conviction ef Samuel Hunter on connection with the Salford gas frauds was not a case in which he could advise any remission of sentence. The England and Wales Census Bill and the Scotland Census Bill went through committee, and were read a third time and passed. THE ANGLO-GERMAN AGREEMENT. Sir JAMES PERGUSSON, in moving the second reading of the Anglo-German Agreement Bill, said that by the agreement with Germany we had obtained the fullest security for our possessions in Africa and such further expansion as was necessary to our interest; and arrange- ments had also been made with France. Mr. GLADSTONE said he considered it his duty to give unqualified credit to Lord Salisbury for the way in which he had set about this agreement. Mr. Gladstone then expressed -himself strongly regarding the inexpediency of one statesman holding the offices of Prime Minister and Foreign Secre- tory, and said he was afraib the pressure of subjects of I anxiety had led to difficulty in this case. He pointed out that in the whole course of its exist- ence the House of 'Commons had never before been adked to vote the cession of territory. In scores of cases cession had taken place, and in each case the practice 'had been uniform. It had been for the Ministry to advise on their responsibility, for the Crown to act on that advice, and for Parliament to accept the result. Through this change in the treaty-making power it might at some time come to pass that the action of the House of 'Lords would be out of harmony with what a 'Liberal Government might conceive to be due tothe wishes of the people. He could not vote against the bill, for it had been -promised to the German Emperor in a treaty whichher Majesty was quite competent to make, but he could not be a party to creating this precedent, and therefore could not tAke part in the proceed- ings on the bill. He valued the British Consti- tution, and 'would not touch it except upon good cause. 'Mr. Goscmarl said it was the Crown that had stipulated for the assent of Parliament in this instance. Sir "Whtmom HARCOURT said the present 'proceeding on the face of it destroyed the treaty-making • power of the Crawn,and the result of making Parliament a party to treaties would be that any• treaty which the 'House of Lords did not approve could not be proceeded with. After some remarks'by 'Mr. Balfour, Sir HORACE 'DAVEY said the action of the Government was a precedent of the most dangerous character, for which not one Shred of justification had been shown. Mr. PHILIPPS moved the rejection of the bill. A lengthy discussion having taken -place. Mr. Sams wished to move the -closure, but the Speaker was of opinion that further dis- cussion ought to be permitted, and the debate was adjourned ta the neat day. The House went into Committee on the Public Works -Loans Bill, but at 12 o'clock the debate stmod adjourned. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Reports cf Supply of the 17th and 18th July (With the exception of the Prisons vote) ere agreed to. 'The'Postage Rates Bill was withdrawn.. The Life and Property'Protection Bill was read a second time. "TTII6 House adjourned ab twenty-Ave minutes to one.

'Since his arrival in London, Sir William Whiteway has had several interviews with Lord Salisbury in further- ance of the settlement of the diMculty with respect to thl,Newfoundland Fisheries. We understand that the Newfoundland Premier has intimated to Lord Salisbury the readiness of his Government to modify or repeal the Acta forbidding the supply of bait to the French fisher- meni if France will withdraw the system of bounties whh operate to the disadvantage of the Newfoundland fishermen in foreign snatirePs.

A debate, at once animatolL and protracted, 'took place upon the schedule fixing the scale of pensions -for the constabulary of the metroptais. Mr. Burdett-Coutts moved that. the maximum of two-thirds ,pay demanded by the men should he. conceded. The 'Home Secretary, I however, emphatically objected to the amendment, which, on a division. mas negatived by-sixteen votes to sewn. Then Mr. Baum:tin proposed that the two-thirds should be attained gaf',er twenty-six years' service, whereupon Mr. Matthews.oas a compromise, suggested a scale of pro- portions under which the men would secure like two- thirds on the completion of twenty-seven yearAtervbe. This arrangeznent met with the approval of Moe Com- mittee, and, amid cheers, the 'Bill was ordered Ito be reported tolit.o House.

div.head: ZANZIBAR PROTECTOUTE.
div.p: THE ZANZIBAR PROTECTOUTE.

CONCESSIONS TO FRANCE. Paws, NEDNESDAY.—WitIia reference to the negotia- tions between Great Britain And France conceiving the compensation to be given tsithe latter country or the establishment of a British protectorate over Zanzibar, the " Figare'" this morning announces that two points appear now to be settled, first, the British Goverfunent admits the right of France to grant an exequatur to foreign consuls in Madagascar through the intermediary of the French resident generaL and secondly, Great Britian admits the principle of a rectification of the frontiers of Senegambia and the per Niger territory, and assents to the extension of French influence in the region of Lake Thad. The question of a commercial treaty with Tunis,,adds the" Figaro." is kept in reserve by the British Government in order to form the basis for further negotiations with regard to the settlement of the French claims respecting Newfoundland. • The negotiations between Lord Salisbury and M. Ribot are being "actively prosecuted." It is semi-officially announced that M. Ribot "absolutely" refused to allow the" rights" of France in Newfoundland a,ud Zanzibar to be discussed.

The Borough Treasurer's report on the receipts' and expenditure of the Corporation of Warrington from the 26th March, 1889, to the 25th March, 1890. has been issued this week. It is a volume of 200 pages, priated by Messrs. John Walker & Co., at the • Examiner" office, and gives in detail the monetary transactions of the Corporation during the period named.

div.head: BOROUGII RATE FUND ACCOUNT.

div.head: _ MR. CAINE AND EAST BRADFORD.
div.p: _ MR. CAINE AND EAST BRADFORD.

Mr. W. S. Caine has accepted an invitation to address the Gladstonian Liberal Two Hundred of East Bradford, with a view to opposing Mr. Byron Reed, the Conserva- tive member at the next election. In an interview with a representative of the press, Mr. Caine said: 4‘ I know Bradford well, have had intimate friendships with its leading men, and flatter myself, from having already fought two Yorkshire constituencies, that I am well acquainted with the sturdy independence of the typical Yorkshireman, in whom are mirrored so many of the 'stalwart' ideas I have worked so long to promote. I could not wish for better things than to represent East Bradford; it is an ideal constituency—ideal in so far as I have a great liking for the men who would help me to win. But I am alighting man, ready and willing to throw myself into the thicxest of the strife where there is a chance of carrying my principles to victory. I have had invitations from all parts of the country, but my ground will always be north of the Trent."
MARRIAGE OF THE HEADMASTER OF
RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOLS.

A marriage which created considerable interest took place at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, on Tuesday. the contracting parties being Mr. John Ford Moulton, schoolmaster, and Isabella, eldest daughter of Mr. William Shields, chemical engineer, Waterloo-road, Runcorn. The circumstances attend- ing the happy event were most auspicious, the sun shone brilliantly, and everything passed off with the eclat which should always characterise affairs of this description. Ten o'clock was the hour fixed for the nuptial ceremony. A great number of friends were attracted to the chapel to witnesS the interesting pro- ceedings, and to greet the bride and bridegroom with those cordial good wishes which betoken sincere affection and esteem. The relatives, and others of the wedding party, began to assemble in good time, and at five minutes to tea the bridegroom appeared, accompanied by his best man, Mr. Hugh Hughes, the famous captain of the premier Cheshire football club. Happily there was not long to wait, for with commendable punctuality Miss Shields, leaning on the arm of her father, passed up the aisle to the communion rail. She carried in her hand a most lovely boquet of flowers. The marriage ceremony was very impressively performed by the Rev. W. Kendrew. At the close of the service, the bridal party repaired to the vestry, after which the newly wedded pair passed down the aisle to the carriages, and were greeted with showers of rice for good luck. The whole of the party proceeded to the residence of the ' bride's father, which was the scene of the remainder of the day's festivities. Having bade their friends farewell, the happy pair left, amid renewed congratulations and hearty wishes for their happiness, for County Down, their intention being to spend the honeymoon among the Mourne mountains. Among the numerous presents which were given was one from the teachers, scholars, and officials of the Board, consisting of a beautiful dinner service, and a silver cruet stand, accompanied by an address wishing him 'to accept the wedding gift as a token of their regard and esteem. They also asked him to accept their best wishes for his future happiness throughout his married life. In acknowledging the pre- sent, Mr. Moulton asked them to accept his sincere and hearty thanks for the handsome present they were pleased to give him. He did not value the gift for its intrinsic value but as an evidence of their kindly feeling towards him.

div.head: LORD It. O.III.TRaIi.ILL AT A TORY DINNER.
div.p: LORD It. O.III.TRaIi.ILL AT A TORY DINNER.

Lord Randolph Churchill, speaking at a dinner at the Conservative Club in London on Wedaesday night, said he regarded the manner in which the toast of his health had been received as indicating that justice and charity were still qualities predominating inConseryative minds, and that the operations of time and the exercise of thought hid modified previous judgments, which were possibly hasty and partial. The Conservative cause re- presented a living and stimulating ideal, containing, as it did, the preservation in integrity and fulness of a great agglomeration of liberty, powers and wealth con- centrated in these isles. The Conservative party was animated in its hopes and aims by a great political prin- ciple, and although the party was willing and anxious to sacrifice much for the sake of Ireland, Parliamentary union of the kingdom was the point upon which they must insist. Adverse by-elections, barren sessions, and the temporary disarray of the party could not shake that immortal principle.

div.head: LOCAL BOWLING.
div.p: LOCAL BOWLING.
MATCH FOR £4O.

On Monday, at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay (proprietor. Mr. Dutton), W. Pilkington, of St. Helens, and W. Gleave, of Warrington, played a match at 71 points up for £2O aside. About 200 persons witnessed the game, which finally resulted in favour of °leave by nine points, the full scores being—Gleave, 71; Pilkington, 62. MAIN ON THE BANK QUAY GREEN. A main at bowls, for 64 players. open to all Eng- land, was concluded on Saturday on the Bank Quay Bowling Green. It was commenced on the Thurs- day previous, and should have been finished last evening week, but owing to a heavy downpour of rain on that day it was postponed until the Satur- day. The game was 13 up, and as there were several attractive prizes the entries were of a good order, and the attendance was satisfactory. The following took the four principal prizes :-1, J. T. Massey; 2, j. Middleton; 3, Joseph Gleave; and 4, W. Dutton. The two latter were equal.

div.head: X.A
div.p: X.A
STARVED TO DEATH.

- A married woman named Mary Wyper has been appre- hended by the Wrexham police on a charge of causing the death of her female child, aged five months, by starva- tion. At the inquest on the body on Wednesday the medical gentleman who had made a post-mortem examina- tion of the body, stated that, in his opinion, the child had been two or three days without food prior to its death.

div.head: DROWNED AT THE ISLE OF MAN.
div.p: DROWNED AT THE ISLE OF MAN.

• A young man named Manning, from Manchester city, was bathing on Wednesday at Dalby, near Peel, in the Isle of Man, when he became exhausted in the rough sea and cried for help. His companions had reached the beach with difficulty; but one of the party, Ernest Catling, hurriedly went to his rescue, throwing out a rope. It failed to reach him, however, and the unfor- tunate young man sank, and was drowned in the presence of his friends, several of whom were ladies. -- • ---

div.head: BURGLAR HIRES A SPECIAL TRAIN.
div.p: A BURGLAR HIRES A SPECIAL TRAIN.

The Farnham magistrates on Tuesday committed two men named Allan and Hyde for trial at the Hants As- sizes for burglary. An extraordinary feature of the case was that Allan induced the South-Western Railway Co. to run him a special train from Waterloo to Southamp- ton the night before the burglary, for which he paid with a fictitious cheque. After committing the burglary and hiding a quantity of plate in a cornfield, he went with a companion to a neighbouring house, partook of breakfast, thanked the lady of the house profusely, and handed her a cheque for £7OO for the courtesy she had shown them.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

SHOCKING MANSLAUGHTER. At the Londonderry Assizes, on Monday, William Woods, rag gatherer, was convicted of the manslaughter of his paramour, and was sentenced to twelve years' penal servitude. The prisoner first tied a cord round the woman's neck, and then nearly severed her head with a scythe.

THE DANGER OF WAKES. From the South of Ireland, on Monday, it was reported that another epidemic of fever had broken out on Hare Island in the Skibberdeen Union, which has been already the scene of so much devastation by epidemics. It is supposed to have originated at the wake of a man who died of fever, the people then mixing freely together. The doctor's direction to remove the patient to hospital was disregarded.

div.head: PLEURO-PNEUMONIA OUTBREAK.
div.p: THE PLEURO-PNEUMONIA OUTBREAK.

Pleuro-pneumonia is spreading in various parts of the country, which means a serious loss to the farmers and to the ratepayers. The stamping-out process has commenced in earnest in Yorkshire, where on Saturday an order was given to carry out the slaughter of 124 beasts on one farm which had been in contact with an animal which died of the dreaded disease. This will probably mean a cost of .£1,200 or .£1,500 to the County Council. The area of the disease appears to be spreading, and the "stamping out' attempt will be proportionately vigorous.

WARRINGTON. It was thought that the vigilance exercised by the sanitary officials in Warrington had not only completely overcome the disease so far as the borough is concerned, but had prevented any likelihood of there being any further outbreak. Unfortunately this has not proved to be the case, as, in spite of all the measures taken by the authorities, another outbreak is reported, this time on the premises of Mr. William Ford, cowkeeper, 5, Marsh- house-lane. One milking cow was found to be affected, and it and another animal which had been in contact with it were cn Tuesday destroyed, by order of the sani- tary authority. This is the only outbreak of the disease in the borough since the 19th June last. The animals destroyed were valued at about £3O. In consequence of the prevalence of pleuro-pneumonia in the Wigan and Warrington districts, the Board of Agriculture have declared a great portion of them to be infected areas. The order took effect yesterday. PADGATE. Twenty-three cattle, belonging to Mr. William Bennett, of Padgate, which had been in contact with infected animals, have this week been destroyed by order of the local authority. It is expected that thelremainder of the 95 condemned animals on this farm will be slaughtered in the course of a few weeks. Mr. Bennett has been very unfortunate, as no fewer than 44 animals were killed only a short time ago by order of the authorities, as they were reported to have been in contact with others suffer- ing from pleuro-pneumonia. The amount of compensa- ion to be paid to Mr. Bennett will, therefore, be excep- tionally large. OUTBREAK AT RAINHILL. On Monday morning, a report was received by the Clerk of the Lancashire County Council, that pleuro- pneumonia had broken out in a herd of forty-nine cattle on the Rainhill Asylum farm. One animal had already been slaughtered, and it was probable that the whole herd would have to be similarly dealt with.

div.head: DUNLO DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: THE DUNLO DIVORCE CASE.

In the Divorce Divison, on Wednesday, before Sir James Hannen and a special jury, the suit of Dunlo v. Dunlo and Wertheimer came on for hearing. This was a petition of Lord Dunlo, son of the Earl of Clancartv, for the dissolution of his marriage by reason of the alleged adultery of his wife, who is better known as Miss Belle Bilton,an actress, with Mr. Isidore Werthei- mer. Answers were filed denying the charges, and the respondent pleaded connivance if there was any adultery. Sir Ckarles Russell, in opening the case for the petitioner, said that Lord Dunlo was the son of the Earl of Clancarty, and was a young man who attained his majority at the ena of 1889. The respondent was a lady some years his senior in point of age and very much his senior in point of ex- perience,of the world. She was described as a lady of considerable attractions and talent, and had for some time followed the calling of a singer at various halls. the acquaintance between the petitioner, Lord Dunlo, and the respondent began about May, 1889, and con- tinued from May till June, the petitioner being in the habit of visiting her at that place on several occasions, and passing the night or portions of the night there. His father, fearing that he had got into bad company, resolved to send him on a • voyage round the world in company with Mr. Robinson, M.A. However, he was surprised to read in the newspaper an announcement of the marriage of his son on the 10th July, 1889. Lord Clancarty insisted that as his son was not of age he should remain under his care, and go abroad as arranged. Accordingly Lord Dunlo, after living with the defendant until the 15th July, went abroad on that date. Lady Dunlo appeared to have given her consent to his going. The respondent was charged with adultery with a person named Werth- eimer, who was described as the son of a well-known bric-a-brac dealer in Bond-st. It was important to state what her relations with co-respondent were before her marriage. In May, 1888, they found that she was ac- quainted with Mr. Wetheimer and with a Mr. Weston. In July, 1888, she was living under the protection of Wertheimer at Farley Lodge, Maidenhead, which was taken by Wertheimer for her. On the 25th lily, 1888, she was confined. Mr. Wertheimer made the arrange- ments for the accouchement. The child was ultimately registered as the son of Walter A. Weston, and one of the names given to it was Isidore. After the confinement the respondent and co-respondent travelled and lived together at the same hotels, and spent their time in each other's company. In the autumn of 1888 they returned to London, and in October or November of that year the respondent returned to London, and at the end , of 1888 or the beginning of 1889 the co-respondent took a house at St. John's Wood, and there he either lived with the respondent or visited her up to the time when she made the acquaintance of Lord Dunlo. In the spring of 1889 it appeared that Wertheimer's iends also wished • to relieve him of entanglement; and he was sent tc: America. The marriage of Lord Dunlo took place on the 10th of July. On the 18th of July Wertheimer returned from America, and visited the respondent at the Hotel Victoria, where she was staying, Lord Dunlo then having taken his departure. The •fact was that respondent and co-respondent lived the life they had lived before Wertheimer had been sent abroad by his friends. Lord Dunlo's friends had them watched, and at the end of December he was requested to sign a petition for divorce. He at first declined to believe what was alleged against his wife, but eventually the petition was filed. The respondent had pleaded that petitioner had left her with- out support after living with her at the Hotel Victoria, and had gone to Australia, and had never since cohabited with her or cantributed to her support. Lord Dunlo then gave evidence in support of his petition The case was resumed on Thursday, when a page de. posed to Mr. Wertheimer visiting Lady Dunlo at St. John's Wood, and a private inquiry agent described their movements in company from the 19th July onwards. The witness read out the dates from a book he had before him. In cross-examination, witness said he had destroyed the diary in which original entries were made. The President pointed out that the present book was no corroboration. Lord Clancarty (examined), said he had arranged for his son to go away 1 efore he heard of the marriage. He had received a letter from Lady Dunlo appealing to him regarding unfounded rumours cir- culated about her, but it remained unanswered.

div.head: GRENADIER GUARDS.
div.p: THE GRENADIER GUARDS.

The Tamar, troopship, with the 2nd Battalion of the Grenadier Guards on board, put into Spithead on Wed- nesday morning for the embarkation of the wives and families of some of the men and the baggage. The heavy baggage was taken to the trooper at Spithead in the Pike and Magnet gunboats, the lighter baggage being reserved for conveyance with the. 22 women and 32 child- ren who came from London by an ordinary afternoon train,in which two or three ofscers, with their wives and children, also travelled. The majority of the married women are not on the strength of the regiment, and some of those who are failed to pass the medical examination. The Tamar got away about 5 o'clock, going down the Solent and by the Needles passage into the Channel. The captain left with sealed orders, which are not to be opened before Thursday, but that Bermuda is his destina- tion has been announced on official authority. There was a large crowd to witness the Guards leave London; i and there s a feeling that those who have been sent to prison for the late expression of dissatisfaction have been hardly used.

div.head: RACE WEER AT NEWTON.
div.p: RACE WEER AT NEWTON.

The annual races at Newton Common commenced on Thursday, and as the weather was beautifully fine there was an immense influx of visitors and excursionists from all parts of the country. Many thousands of " racing characters" arrived from Liverpool, Manchester, and intermediate places, and about noon and in the evening the roads to theracecourse were thronged by horses, cabs, traps, waggonettes, and vehicles of every description. The vicinity of .the rail- way was animated and thronged by almost every class of people, and it is satisfactory to record that everything passed off without any mishap. The races are the occa- sion for stopping the leading works in the district. "Race-week 'has for many years been recognised as the principal holiday in the district, and nearly all the works closed, on Thursday at noon, until next Monday morning. Following the custom of former years, the scholars attending the Sunday schools in the town were entertained to their annual field-day. The scholars paraded the principal streets of the town. The Baptists subsequently proceeded to a field in Crow-lane, belonging to Mr. Sanderson; the Wesleyans spent the afternoon in Mr. Sanderson's field near the works of Messrs. Vicars and Sons, the Primitive Methodists were taken to a field belonging to Mr. J. Worsley near the Nine Arches, Burtonwood, and the Congregationalists marched to a field in Ashton-road. Happily the weather throughout the day was extremely fine and the scholars seemed to heartily enjoy themselves, without excep- tion.

UNWELCOME VISITORS. One of the most forbidding features of the races is that of bringing into the neighbourhood A consider- able number of offenders against the law. Some dozens of policemen are drafted into Earlestown, Newton and surrounding district during the con- tinuance of the races, but though they are generally of an active disposition they cannot be expected to detect all offenders. Some, however, do fall into their "clutches," as on Thursday afternoon, when three men named John Thompson, John Byrom, and John Oakes, were brought before Mr. F. J. Gillespie, JP., at a special court held in the Earlestown Police Station. Thompson wks charged with playing the "card trick," and the other two were charged with gaming with a box and numbers. Police Sergeant Longworth, of Newton- le-Willows, proved these cases, and said in Byrom's possession two "flash "notes were found, and Oakes had the sum of 214-s. I.ld. Thompson and Byrom were- each fined 103. and costs, and Oakes was fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: ELECTION OF -COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF -COMMISSIONERS.
LIVELY SCENES.

The election of three commissioners for the township of Newton, took place on Wednesday, and was productive of some lively proceedings. The• three retiring members were Messrs. C. B. F. Borron (glass-bottle manufacturer), James Fairclough (corn miller), and Thomas Hunt (farmer), and they were nominated for re-election. Under circum- stances narrated in our last issue, the Earlestown ratepayers "rose in arms" against the action of the- Board upon several questions, and at a public Meeting held on Monday week, in the Co-operative Hall, it was unanimously decided to bring out • Messrs. Thomas Ormand, E. T. Evans, and P. McMahon, as ratepayers' candidates, in opposition to the retiring members. Messrs. Henry Hibbert and J. E. Pardey, both of Newton, were also nominated, but Mr. Pardey early withdrew from the contest, leaving the battle for the three vacant seats to the seven candidates who decided to go to the poll. The result of the keenest and most exciting contest which has ever occurred in connection with the appoint- ment of Commissioners was that the three Earlestown gentlemen Messrs. Ormond, McMahon, and Evans, were elected by large majorities, and their success was a very popular one to the usually demonstrative Earlestown ratepayers. On the day of polling the interest in the contest was general. The votes were taken in the assembly-room of the Town Hall, Newton, between the hours of nine in the morning and four in the afternoon, and during the whole of that period the Returning Officer (Mr. B. B. Glover) and other officials were kept busy in registering the votes of ratepayers. Mr. Glover, in the performance of his duties, was assisted by Mr. R. Brierley (presiding officer), Mr. J. E. Worsley (law clerk), Mr. H. Hough- ton (assistant overseer), and Mr. F. Brierley (poll clerk), while Mr. T. Unsworth acted as agent on behalf of Messrs. Ormond, Evans, and McMahon; Mr. J. H. Moscrop occupying a similar position on behalf of Messrs. Borron, Fairclough, and Hibbert. The first three voters were Messrs. J. Adams, J. Parr, and J. Hughes, and they were followed by a constant stream of ratepayers. Each side had a full staff of active workers, and an entirely new feature were the respective committee rooms on each side of High-street, near the Town Hall. These were the scenes of much bustle and animation. There were many traps and vehicles used to convey voters from Earlestown and other distant parts of the township, and they were freely utilised by the ratepayers. After the poll had closed, the Town Hall was thrown open for the usual meeting to pass the Commissioners' accounts, and to receive the official de- claration of the result of the polling. A large number of persons crowded into the room. About half an hour after the voting ceased the figures were announced by the returning officer. Mr. J.W. Emmett (chairman of the Board of Commissioners) occupied the chair, and among , those present were Messrs. B. B. Glover (returning officer), W. F. Gooch, J. Fairzilough, C.B. F. Borron, G. Ratcliffe, T. Hunt, T. Foster, R. Bell, G. Clarke, T. Ormand, P. Thompson, J. Prescott, B. Harrison, J. H. Graham, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. Brierley (sur- veyor), Sm. Mr. B. B. Glover declared the result of the poll to be as follows : Mr. Ormand Mr. McMahon ,„,„„ 1,024 Mr. Evans ..... Oll/N

After the declaration had been made, the chatrmanP- called upon the three gueusful owdidates to speak.- Mr. T. Orn3od 4. td the three candidates who had 'men, elected. I,M.e deeply indebted to those who had supnortedt them for the able and efficient manner in which" they had come up to the poll to record their votes. As their representatives on the Board of Commissioners they would feel it their bounden duty to do their best for the interests of the whole township impartially. To those who had worked on behalf of himself and Messrs. McMahon and Evans, their heartiest thanks were due. They were thankful for the kind and cordial feel- ing which had been exhibited by both sides in the contest. (Cheers.)—Mr. C. B. F. Borron thanked the 831 electors who had recorded their votes in his favour, and thosc friends who had worked so hard for him. If the electors wished his services on any future occasion, he should be glad to place them at their dis- posal. (Applause.)—Mr. Fairclough also thanked those who had supported him, and Mr. Hibbert said it was the first time ho had gone to poll and he was not ashamed of the result. He hoped that on the next occasion his claims for election would be more favourably received. —Mr. T. Hunt said during his past connection with the Newton Improvement Commissioners he had always tried to do his duty. He could see that the election had been simply a political strife, and his (Mr. Hunt's) chances tf re-election were minimised by a report that he was about to retire. He had to fight his battle single- handed, and under those circumstances he never had much hope of success. Nevertheless, he thanked the few electors who had voted for him. (Applause.) The Chairman then moved a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. 'B. 13. Glover for his services as returning officer in the election. He said he deserved their thanks for the manner in which the poll had been taken that day. It had been done without the slightest hitch, and the I returning officcr and all connected with him had done their duty remarkably well. The resolution was passed with eheeers. Mr. Glover briefly responded, and remarked that 1,425 votes had been recorded during the day, showing 550 more than at any previous election. (Applause.) He thought that showed that great interest had been taken in the election, and he hoped those who had not been successful would not be disappointed. They should all leave that room as if nothing had happened, and try to redeem their position neet year. (Applause.) The proceedings then terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

The annual Conference in connection with the Congre- eat ional Union of Wales commenced on Tuesday at Eteau- fort, -Afonmoutlishire Th..: subject discussed was Sunday school work, and the speeches revealed that there ii been increased activity in Sunday school effort in the principality recently. They have had " tinii job" in ham4„and they have shown wisdom e's consulting Izapresentative men amongst in the House as to the best course to tale; they woulti have shown moret wisdom jf tboY acted throughout u?on the advice which wq given them, The bulk of the money,. which _ course goes to England, in to be handed over the County Councils, with an intimation that thelY had better be carefai as to what they do with au." seeing that, as soon as legislative manhinerYAc.hy be set up, "there may be new charges br'an,7,,J,.. put upon them in, reference to intermediate, T'eist, nioal,and agricultural education,' it will bore/10d_ bored that Mr, ARTHUR ACLAND moved an alnente ment in this direction when the Goverment °on trying to force the Compensation Clauses liPted the House of Commons; but the Tories so°ll Mr. ACLAND'S suggestion, They will now ht called upon to swallow it in the shape of a draug

div.head: TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: TOUCH AND GO."

Presented to them by the Government themselves, and it is to be hoped they will gulp it down with- out making wry faces. It will be especially nauseous, no doubt, to members of the House of Commons like Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who are in "the trade," and who deemed they were "in the Swim " when they were voting to compensate themselves for a "vested interest" which they do not really possess. It is not quite the same, " stumping up" the taxes on spirits and beer to be applied to educational pur- Posea, as making a pile of them for the brewers, benefit. It is the turn of poor Lazarus to-day; for he is comforted while the rich man is tormented. Intermediate education—thatais very , touch better than the immediate beer-barrel. Wales, wide-awake Wales, has already obtained an Intermediate Education Act, and is now in the happy position of being able to receive her share of the fund and spend it under the new Act. Let • 118 coogratalate her upon being able to take the lead in this matter; and then prepare ourselves to follow her example. Of the £440,000, the sum of 40,000 will be handed over to the Intermediate - Education Board for Ireland, which, as the Chancellor of the Exchequer remarked, " com- • raancls the confidence of the Irish public generally, irrespective of political or religious feeling." This satisfy the representatives of Ireland, and it , has the merit of being in harmony with the pro-

Poaals for England and for Wales. It is Scotland Which is to be subjected to exceptional and Objectionable treatment. The Government's intention as to Scotland's share of the extra spirit and beer duty is that it is not to be applied for education purposes; it is to be handed over to the County Councils for the reduction of rates. Naturally enough, Scotch members are dis- appointed and annoyed at being treated in this Iya37. Their suggestion was, and is, that the ..tO,OOO to which they are entitled should be de- voted to the completion of the scheme of Free Education upon which they have already entered; and Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN has given notice that, at the proper time, he will introduce a motion to this effect. The Government have thus brought a hornet's nest about their ears, and they deserve to be stung for their wrong-headedness. The fact lay they are constitutionally so crooked in their 'ways that they cannot go straight. They are afraid of Scotland having Free Education, out and out, for they know it would hasten the establish- Itent of Free Education throughout the Kingdom. If they were wise, they would do what Scotland desires, and take credit for doing a good thing; but, as they are not wise, they take a wrong yourse and bring discredit upon themselves.
BILL 4 are now before Parliament

• Taking with a view to taking the census - The Census. next year; and on Tuesday evening the measure for England and Wales was under Consideration. It was understood that the Govern- toent stood by the recommendation of the Select Committee, which was that, as heretofore, there Should be no provision for ascertaining the reli- gious opinions of her MAJESTY'S subjects. Baron ThstsnArz, however, moved the addition of a column with the object of ascertaining the reli- gious opinions of the persons enumerated; and, as might be expected, a lively debate ensued. Those who back up the Church as a State institu- tion know very well that a census of this kind would serve their purpose. There are a great Izany people who "go nowhere," who would put themselves down as " Church " if they were re- quired to make a statement on the sub- ject—to say nothing of the class of " worship- Del's " represented by the witty, but back- • 'sliding parishioner who explained that he had ceased to be religious, and had begun go- to Church. Granted that it would be of some interest to know the number of Dissenters, -it.would not be less instructive to know the num- ber of Absenters. Now, if a column was left for this class, it is certain it would be well filled; but, ee it would take from the Church total, it is not of course to be thought of. The truth is,as Sir HENRY JAMES remarked, a religious census is objectionable as an inquisition into men's private opinions. Mr. ItarcHzE, in the course of the debate, gave the 11°use to understand that the amendment was an °Pen question so far as the Government were con- Corned. He was severely taken to task for this by several members of the Opposition, who regarded the intimation as a breach of faith; and Mr. ghtrria, coming in later, threw Mr. RITCHIE over, With the result that the amendment was defeated by a majority of 219 votes. There will be a census hut it will be of the usual kind; it will not require People to ticket themselves as belonging to a par- icular sect.
