The Liberals of St. Helens are to be congratu- lated upon an important addition to their ranks in the person of Mr. S. Taylor, barrister, and lord of the manor of Eccleston. Like many Conservatives, lie has been for some time dissatisfied with the Irish policy of the Government • and, seeing no hope of a change for the better, he has joined the Liberal ranks in the belief that Conciliation and not Coercion is the true policy for Ireland.

The result of the hard-fought contest for the election of three Newton Commissioners is that the three ratepayers' candidates.are at the head of the ion. It will now, it is to be hoped, be acknow- ledged that there was ground for dissatisfaction; and that Earlestown, as the largest district, ought to have fuller representation on the Board. The retiring candidates will not like being snuffed out; and will be inclined to say— You might have dissembled your love, But you needn't have kicked us downstairs.

The pleasure fair at Warrington is almost invari- ably accompanied with one serious accident, and at least half-a-dozen minor accidents. Perhaps it is necessary that someone should be killed before due attention is given to the matter. The fact is, the space set aside for the fair is altogether too small; and, as the town grows larger, the danger increases every year. Matters have got to that pitch that it has become necessary to do one of two things—either provide a larger Fair Ground, or abolish the fair altogether.

The Manchester Ship Canal Company have a keen eye to business in inviting pgrties of traders to inspect the progress of the works. On Wednes- day a most important body, representing some of the principal steam-ship owners of the country, were taken from end to end under the direction of Alderman W. H. Bailey and Mr. Marshall Stevens. As will be seen from our report of the proceedings, the visitors were greatly impressed with the magnitude of the undertaking, and with the rapid progress which has been made.

There has been no little talk in Warrington as to when the Warrington Docks will be commenced; and there are a few " Thomases " who say they will never be made. It has even been said that the Company are under no obligation to construct docks at Warrington; and there is a disposition to blame the Corporation for lack of foresight and energy in the matter. However, it is something toknow that the law requires that the docks "shall" be made, and that the Company are limited as to time.

The clause in the Ship Canal Act of 1885 which refers to the subject runs as follows:—"The Com- pany shall, within the period of three years after the completion of the Canal between Eastham and Latchford, and the opening of the same for traffic, construct at Warrington, on the site shown on that behalf on the deposited plans, or such other site within the limits of deviation as may be agreed on between the Corporation and the Com- pany, the dock shown on the said plans." The language of the clause is involved; but, simply stated, it means that the Warrington docks must be made within three years of the opening of the Canal between Eastham and Latchford.

-- Two civil servants have been severely punished for having dared to interview Mr. Goschen relative to dissatisfuction in the Customs' department. One of them (Mr. F. G. Heath) loses £2O a year, and is not to be again promoted, and the other (Mr. Smith) has his annual increase stopped. A fine of £2O a year—for a breach of discipline—is mons- trous. A eat may look at a King; but a servant, however "civil," must not speak to a Chancellor of the Exchequer. Toryism, as of old, is another name for tyranny.

The Postmaster-General was taken to task in the House of Commons, on Wednesday,for his conduct towards his subordinates. Sir E. J. Reed told Mr. Raikes point blank that "the difficulty which had arisen at the Post Office was in consequence of his treating the men under his orders as slaves." It was admitted that there was a right on the part of postmen to combine in their own interests; but it was shown that the Postmaster-General sought to frighten them out of their combination by arbitrary restrictions. A plea was made for the reinstation of the men dismissed for taking part in the strike; and it is to be hoped it will not be without effect.

Mr. Hanbury shows himself more independent than the ordinary supporters of the Government, and he is deserving of thanks for having something to say in the House of Commons on behalf of the Grenadier Guards. He sticks to his statement as to the officers neglecting to salute their men; and urges that " officers of the Guards, like the regi- ments of the line, should live in barracks with their men." It is not denied that the disaffected Guards had cause of complaint; and the opinion is pretty general that the officers have been screened, whilst the men have been too severely punished.

Wales is working hard to get the Disestablish- ment question to the front, and the matter has been under the consideration of the General Pur- poses Committee of the National Liberal Federa- tion. Their recommendation is "that, at the next annual meeting of the Federation, Welsh Disestab- lishment shall be dealt with in a separate resolution, which resolution shall stand next on the agenda to the motion on Irish Home Rule; the Manchester resolution to be further so amended as to read— 'should be dealt with in the next Parliament, as soon as Irish Home Rule is attained.'" This will do; there is nothing heats "Keep pegging away" if you want to get a thing done.

The Tories always call themselves the constitu- tional party, and they are always showing that they know little about the Constitution. They had to drop their: proposal to ear-mark the spirit duty, because it was unconstitu- tional; and now, as Mr. Gladstone showed on Thursday night, they are violating constitutional practice by interfering with the treaty-making powers of the Crown in the cession of Heligoland. If a Liberal government had sought to limit the prerogative of the Sovereign, it would have been pronounced disloyal. Is it disloyal for the Tories to take this course, or is it merely another evidence of their constitutional stupidity?

As a sequel to the death from blood-poisoning at Davenham, Dr. Fox, Medical Officer of Health, has been denouncing barbed-wire fencing. He suggested to the Northwich Rural Sanitary Authority that they should try to induce Parlia- ment to render it illegal to place such fencing at the side of a footpath or highVvay. Something ought to be done, but the " ruralists " of Northwich are not the men to do it. Some of them have a "sneaking regard" for the barbed wire; and the Clerk pointedly remarked that there were lads in Northwich who would get over anything but a I barbed wire fence. And so to keep the boys out, upgrown people must continue to take their chance of being maimed or poisoned.

It is the Dissentients now who are trying to get the Premier to again take Lord Randolph Churchill into the cabinet. They are afraid, if he does not go to prop up the ministry,Lord Harting- ton must; and then, what will become of the Dis- sentients? They will be discarded as so many Tories. But Lord Salisbury doesn't as yet take to the proposal. It is not that his love of the Dis- sentients is little, but that his hatred of "Randy" is great. He compared him, when he was in the cabinet to a carbuncle on one's neck; and he has not yet got to wanting that carbuncle back again.

Lord Randolph had a dinner given him by his Tory friends on Wednesday; and ha made them a sort of sitting-on-the-fence speech. Amongst other things he said :—" You and I, gentlemen, may occasionally differ with Her Majesty's Govern- ment. We may occasionally either in public or in

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 26, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 26, 1890.

private criticise it. I may criticise expenditure, and I may censure the appointment of the Parnell Commission. You may complain of the introduc- tion of the licensing law reform into the Govern- ment programme, you may lament the legislative failure of this session. You and I may think that we occasionally discern some insufFciency of skill in the management of business, or some insuffi- ciency of determination on the part of the Govern- ment to adhere to a position deliberately taken up. But when we come to think of giving judgment upon the conduct of the Government, we take the career as a whole." Just so; "we take that career as a whole," and we say that it fully deserves the fate which is in store for it the General Elec- tion.

RUNCORN FREEMASONS AT LLANDUDNO. The members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons held their annual picnic on Thursday, when a most en- joyable day was spent at Llandudno. SIMMS CROSS. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CILS,PEL, WIDNES. The annual. sermons were preached in this place of worship on Sunday-, by the Rev. W. Jackson, of Leeds. There were good congregations at each service, and collections were made in aid of the trust funds. On the previous evening (Saturday) the rev, gentleman had delivered his popular lecture on "Working together and .its fruits."

BUTTON BOARD SCROOL EMCDRSION. Through the liberality and kindness )f ladies and gentlemen in the neighbourhood, the children attending the Dutton Board School had their annual trip to the sea- side on Monday. The place choaen this year was South- port, and the parents and scholars,to the number of 100, left Pteston Brook at nine in the morning. Every arrangement had been made for the pleasure and com- fort of the party, and a pleasant day was spent. OXFORD UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUN- -

CORN. Arrangements have been made for two courses of lectures during the coming winter. In the first course commencing on October aud, Mr. Hubert Lllwellyn Smith, 8.A., B. Sc., will deal with the subject of " Wealth and industry." The second course commences hi January, and Mr. H. J. Mackinder, M.A., will lecture on "The making of nations, or the history of geography of international politics." The charges will probably be the same as last year.

SCHOOL TREATS AT RUNCORN. \ The children attending Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School, with a number of parents and friends, spent a pleasant afternoon on Overton Hills on Wednesday. The party, numbering about 700 persons, were conveyed to and from Frodsham by special train. Tea was provided at Mersey View.—On Tuesday, the scholars connected with Holy Trinity Church also spent the afternoon on Overton Hills at Mersey View. About 350 persons were conveyed in the special train which was chartered. On Wednesday, the infants had their treat, spending a happy time in a field lent by Mrs. C. Hazlehurst. AN UNGRATEFUL YOUTH AT RUNCORN. Before Major Hazlehurst and Dr. Steele, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, a youth 16 years of age, named Win. Smith, alias Win. John Owen, was charged with stealing a guernsey, the property of Evan Evans. Evans was a hand on a schooner, which on the 16th June was lying in Runcorn Docks. The prisoner went on board and said he had nowhere to go, and he was given his tea and allowed to sleep on the schooner at night. Next morning he decamped with the guernsey, which he after- wards pawned at Storer's in High-st. Superintendent Large said the prisoner had been brought up on the training ship "Clio," which he had left with a good character. The Bench discharged the prisoner, on his promising to behave better in future, and to come up for judgment when called upon. ASSAULTS AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, a young man named James Scally, was charged with assaulting Lawrence Keegan, who keeps a lodging house in Marsh- st.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant.—Scally and his wife lodged with Keegan and on Saturday after- noon the latter ejected Mrs. Scatty from the house because she had used threats to his wife. Afterwards the defendant came to the house, and kicked Keegan in the pit of the stomach and also struck him on the chest. As Keegan was a delicate man, suffering from consump- tion, he had since been very unwell. The defendant also smashed three panes of glass.—The defendant alleged that he and his wife were ill-used by Keegan and his wife and that the former cut his arm by throwing a glass at him.—The Bench bound him over to keep the peace for three months.—Mrs. Keegan was then charged with assaulting Annie Purcell,a young unmarried woman. It I was alleged that the defendant had thrown stones at the complainant, had torn hair from her head and generally illtreated her. The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. THE SCHOONER MARGARET, from Runcorn for Rio de Janeiro, laden with coal, was put in dock at Bahai on Monday with loss of all sails. SummEte SALE DOH On at J & W. DUTTON'S Saukey-at., Warrington.—Advt. DEATH OF A CHESHIRE LADY. Intelligence has been received at Norley, near Frodsham, of the death, at Hardwicke Court, near Gloucester, of Mrs. Lloyd Baker, daughter of the Hon. A. Lascelles, of Norley.

BICYCLE ACCIDENT. A boy named Naylor, residing at Parr, met with a serious accident on Saturday night. He was playing in Higher Parr-st., when Frederick Apple- ton, a young man, residing at Sankey, came up on a bicycle. Naylor was knockod down and was badly cut about the legs and face. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, Ban Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, AtIII. tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Union, American, and ' other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner' Office, Bewsev-st.. Warrington.—Advt. IMPROVING THE NAVIGATION OF THE BEE. The River Dee Conservancy Board are construct- ing two expensive groins or causeways by the Rock Channel, below Connah's Quay for the purpose of removing an enormous sandbank which has formed there, and to turn the channel from the Welsh to the English coast. Within the past few days two Norwegian vessels have gone aground there' the Magda having had a narrow escape from total loss. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT COLLINS GREEN COLLIERY.

Two men named John Shaw and Thomas Murray, employed as day wagemen in Collins Green No. 1 Pit, met with a serious accident on Monday. They were engaged repairing the roof, when it suddenly gave way, and a large quantity of earth and stones fell upon them. They were seriously injured and were at once taken up the shaft and removed to the Providence Hospital, St. Helens, where they remain as in-patients. Mn. I. S. LEADAN'S CANDIDATURE OF THE ALTRINCIIAM Speaking on Wednesday night at the Sale Liberal Club, Mr. 1. S. Leadam (Gladstonian Liberal candi- date for tke Altrincham Division) said the meeting between the Government and the nation at the next election would be a meeting between the be- trayers and the betrayed. Ile contended that local government was impossible in Ireland under the present regime, and that the English nation had de- cided to retrace its steps and abandon the course it entered upon at the last election.

THE MUZZLING ORDER IN CHESHIRE. At a meeting of the Cheshire Standing Joint Com- mittee, held at Chester, on Saturday, Mr. Howard asked if any action was being taken respecting the Muzzling Order. Mr. Lister replied that at a meet- ing of the Contagious Diseases Animals Committee, it was agreed to recommend to the Board of Agriculture that they should relax the muzzling order, so as to allow dogs to go unmuzzled provided they wore a collar bearing the name and address of the owner. The order, he added, would, they hoped, come into force almost directly. SUMMER SALE now on at J. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adrt.

• - TELEPHONIC COMMUNICATION IN CHESHIRE. At the quarterly meeting of the Standing Joint Committee of Cheshire, held on Saturday, Mr. A. K. Dyson proposed a resolution in favour of establish- ing telephonic communication between Sale and Altrincham Police Stations and the main trunk line of the National Telephonic Company ; between Hyde and Dukinfield and the main line, between Egremont and Birkenhead and the main line, be- tween Macclesfield and the main line, between Chester Chief Office and the centre, between Lymm and Altrincham and the main line, between Run- corn and the main line, at a cost of .£125. The motion was seconded by Mr. Speakman, (Runcorn) and unanimously agreed to. THE ILIINFORD MURDER.

Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Ile!ens, who has charge of the defence of Mrs. Pickavance, who is committed for trial with her husband for the mur- der of Mr. Henry Granger Foster, colliery owner, at Rainford, has instructed Mr. M`Keand to defend her at the Liverpool Assizes, which commence's to- day (Saturday.) Messrs. J. O. and W. Swift, the solicitors engaged on behalf of Pickavance. had not instructed counsel on Wednesday, but were ex- pected to do so in the course of a day or two. John D. Pickavana+, who since his committal for trial has been confined at Walton Gaol, was the other day removed to Kirkdale Gaol, where he will be de- tained pending his trial. Mrs. Pickavance, who h ' implicated along with her husband, remains at Walton Gaol.

• -- - - EXCITING TRIP FROM SOUTHPORT. On Wednesday the steamboat Adela, belonging to the Birkdale, Southport, and Preston Steamship Uompany, experienced a rough time of it in at- tempting to cross from Southport to Llandudno. She left the pier head at 11 o'clock in the forenoon, with about 100 passengers on board, and on getting out of the channel encountered strong head winds and heavy seas, the waves repeatedly dashing over her. Portions of her bulwarks near the bow, and also near the paddle-box on the starboard side, were smashed, aid the engine-room flooded with water, the fireman being up to his knees. Ultimately, before Llandudno was sighted, the captain decided to abandon the passage and make for Liverpool, where the bulk of the passengers were landed at half-past two o'clock, to return home by train. SUMMER SALE now on at J. Bc W. Dorros's Saakey-st., Warrington.—Advt. -

DR. DABICZILI WAIERINGTON. As will be seen from our advertising columns, the Rev. Joseph Parker,,D.D., will preach in Wycliffe Church, on Friday week. It is not often that pro- vincial congregations have the opportunity of hear- ing the pastor of the London City Temple; and it is a matter of course to say that Wycliffe Church will be crowded on the occasion of his visit.

SIM APPEARS AGAIN.--. 1 The most notorious police-court " character" a St. Helens is Bridget Kildare, who heads the record for the number of convictions entered in the local police books. On Saturday last, when she was put forward on a charge of sleeping in an outbuilding, she made her 183rd appearance. Bridget was ordered to leave St. Helens for " seven days.'

MR. THOMAS SNAPE, C.C. The" Methodist Times "of this week contains an ad- mirable portrait of Mr. Thomas Snape, C.C., of Widnes, and also an appreciative description of his life and use- fulness in the community. THE HORSE AMBULANCE FOR WIDNES. The Charity Cricket match between Widnes Trades- men and Police, has resulted in a profit of £lO3 2s. 10s. with which it is proposed to purchase a horse ambulance for the hospitals. It is estimated that this will abs4rll about £loo,and the remainder will be devoted to procuring a hand ambulance, for public use, to be kept 4t the police station.

div.head: SUCCESS OF WIDNES MUSICAL STUDENTS.
div.p: SUCCESS OF WIDNES MUSICAL STUDENTS.

The following students of Mr. T. Sherrat, music teacher Widnes, have passed the Trinit3, College (London) local examination in musical knowledge, which was recently held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool :—Miss E. Shores, Bradley Cottage, 87 marks; Miss E. Taylor, Gladstone. street, 78 marks ; Mr. W. Hackney, Town Hall, 80 marks, and Mr. J. Valentine, Warrington-rd., 79 marks. It may be observed that 60 marks entitles a pupil to pass the examination.

POLICE INSPECTION AT RUNCORN. The annual inspection of the police force of the Run- corn Petty Sessional Division was held on Tuesday after- noon by Captain Legge, the Government Inspector. There were on parade Superintendent Large, Inspector Bowyer, four sergeants, and 24 constables,. who were put through drill by Sergeant Woolley. The inspector care- fully examined the clothing and accoutrements of the men, which were all in a highly creditable condition. The cells were visited, and in conclusion the books of the office were thoroughly examined; the result being very satisfactory. 8iT11,9, all kinds.---J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington. Braneh—Barlestown.—Advt.

div.head: THEFT OF A TUMBLER AT HALTON.
div.p: THEFT OF A TUMBLER AT HALTON.

At Runcorn— Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Sweetman, a young man employed on the Ship Canal works, was charged with having stolen a tumbler, worth 3d. from the Halton Castle Hotel on the 14th inst. About nine p.m., P.C. Fryer saw the defendant leave the hotel, and considering his manner suspicious, searched him and found a glass secreted under his coat. The defendant told the cfficer that he had had a glass of beer in it.—The defendant now informed the bench that he had won the glass at a stall which was located near the Inn.—A fine of ss. was imposed. BITTEN BY A MTJZZLED DOG AT WIDNES.

Henry, Edgerley, carter of Appleton-street, was sum- moned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to ans- wer a charge of allowing his dog to be at large insecurely muzzled. A boy named John Keogh deposed that whilst he was near the defendants house, the dog jumped up at his face, and he put up his hand, which was bitten by the animal. The dog had on a leather muzzle.—P.C. Thompson said he examined the dog and found that it could open its mouth from an inch to an inch and a half. It was not wearing a cage muzzle, but a leather muzzle.—The defendant attempted to show that the dog was in the house at the time it was alleged to have bitten the boy.-1 fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed. MAIL CARTS for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt. A RUNCORN BUILDER IN TROUBLE. James Kirkham, builder, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday to answer a charge that he being the builder of dwelling-housPs in Greenway-road and Byrom-st., did fail to give two days notice in writ- ing to the Surveyor of Runcorn Board of Commissioners before certain drains were covered up contrary to the byelaws of the Board.—Defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. F. A. Lake, the law clerk, prosecuted. Mr. Barker, the surveyor, said the drains were put in in a contrary direction to-the manner in which they were marked on the plan and one pipe had been laid which had no con- nection with the drain. The drains were covered up before the necessary notice was given. The defendant said at the time th- pii,as were laid Mr. Barker was on his holidays and ~fendant) instructed his man to put them in temporarily until Mr. Barker returned, intending that if the latter did not approve of the man- ner in which the work was 'done it should be done in accordance with his instructions. Mr. Barker said the drain was not constructed in accordance with the plan and he had promised to have the work done properly.— Mr. Lake said there had been several complaints about the byelaws being Infringed, and he asked the Bench to inflict an exemplary fine. A fine of 20s. and costs was allowed.

div.head: ROW AT HALTON.
div.p: A ROW AT HALTON.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Joseph Rowlands, better known as Porter, was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly at Halton, on the 14th inst. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys defended. Superinten- dent Large said about four o'clock on the date named he saw the defendant near the Elephant and Castle, creating a disturbance with a number of Orangemen with whom he wanted to fight.—P.C. Breeze deposed that at the same place at half-past ten, the defendant and a man named Lydiate were drunk and were making use of bad language. They wanted to fight a young man whom Lydiate struck in the mouth with his fist.—P.S. Costello corroborated. Both officers in cross-examination denied having struck the defendant.—lnspector Bowyer also gave evidence as to the drunkenness.—Evidence was also called to prove that the defendant was sober and quiet. It was alleged that P.S. Costello had struck the defend- ant several times, but the sergeant denied that he did more than push him.—The Bench considered the case proved, and Superintendent Large advised the defendant to be teetotal.—Mr. C. Reynolds: You might try it a bit; you are quiet enough when you are sober. The defend- ant was fined 103. and costs.—The defendant: I am going to promise that the first man who puts his hand on me this year, I am going for with my fist.—Samuel Lydiate then pleaded guilty to being drunk and dis- orderly, and he was fined 10s. and costs. ELECTRO PLATED Goons.—Garland's oldest established Ironmonger, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: SUPPOSED CI.IILD MURDER AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUPPOSED CI.IILD MURDER AT WIDNES.

A shocking discovery was made at Widnes on Sunday morning, the circumstances pointing to a dreadful ease of child murder. About half-past six, a man named Samuel Mercer found in the ashpit of the house 56, Waterloo-road, occupied by Mrs. Clif- ton, the dead body of a newly born male child. He immediately gave information to the police, and the body was carried to the Police Station. After- wards a further search was made; and in the yard of 60, Waterloo-road, occupied by Henry Quinn, there was found a manilla market bass containing a black cardigan jacket and an old wrappering apron, and also a new apron of the same material. The articles were covered with blood. On Tues- day !qr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Police Court. Superintendent Noblett described the circumstances under which the body was found, and stated that Dr. O'Keeffe had made a post-mortem examination, and he was of opituon that the child was born alive. He pro- poised simply to call evidence of the finding of the body, and then to ask that the inquest should be adjourned for 14 days so that the.police might make further inquiries Into ' the matter. Should anything transpire in the meantime he would ask the coroner to call the jury to- gether at an earlier date.—Samuel Mercer said he was a slater, and lived at 21, Sankey-st., Widnes. On Sunday morning, about half-past six, he was passing down an entry at the rear of some houses, in Waterloo-road, when he saw the dead body of a newly born child, in the ashpit of the house No. 55, occupied by Mrs. Clifton. He drew the attention of P.C. Tweedie to the circum- stances, and together they carried the body to the police station. From the appearance of the child he should say it had been born on the previous night. He did not know who put the body there.—This was the whole of the evidence, and the deputy coroner said the police had good reasons for asking that the inquest should be adjourned.—The inquiry was then adjourned until Tues- day week, August sth.—Up to the present no clue has been discovered which would lead to the finding of the mother, or the person who deposited the infant in the ash-pit.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. AND MRS. H. SUTTON
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MR. AND MRS. H. SUTTON
TIM MIS.

In commemoration of their marriage Mr. and Mrs. H. Sutton Timmis, of Widnes, were the reci- pients of a handsome present from the workpeople of Messrs. W. Gossage and Son on Tuesday. At noon the workmen assembled in the packing room, where appropriate mottoes were displayed, for the pur- pose of witnessing the presentation. Mr. W. Hartland, the oldest employe of the trm, had been deputed by the workmen to perform the ceremony, and in doing so he referred to the kindness and generosity displayed to the people of Widnes by the prin- cipals of the firm in the past. He was glad to see that the young people were following in their footsteps, and were growing up men of able stature, and that they would fulfil all their parents desired them to do, (Ap- plause.) The name of Gossage and Son was spread far and wide, and the name of Timmis would become so universally known that it would almost be necessary to call the firm Gossage and Timmis. (Applause.) He hoped prosperity would attend them all their lives. He was very pleased to meet Mr. H. Sutton Timmis and his dear wife. There was not one of the workmen who did not respect and esteem Mr. Timmis, and when the " old hands "had passed away he hoped the young men would fill their places and be as successful as their fathers had been. (Applause.)—Mr. Hartland then made the presen- tation.—Mr. Timmis, in acknowledging the gift, said he hoped they would realise all the good wishes Mr. Hart- land had expressed. As to the relationship in the firm he only trusted that in the future they would get along as pleasantly as they had done in the past, and try to do their best to keep the firm in the same sound positie4 that it was in now. (Applause.)—Mrs, 11. Timmis also thanked the men for the beautiful things they had given them.—The present Consisted of a handsome set of dish covers, and a case of cutlery, which bore a suitable inscription besides the monogram of the bride and bridegroom .—Mr. Williamson proposed that the best thanks of the worheople be given to Mr. T. S. 'Timmis for his generous gift of £IOD to the funds of the Workmen's Sick and Burial Society. Mr. J. Dux- bury seconded the motion, which was carried with enthusiasm. Mr. Timmis, in reply, said to him and Mr. Gossage it was a pleasure to carry on the business what they 'had good relations with the workpeople. They had no strikes, no trouble, or disagreement with them ; they tried to treat them fairly and considerately and they believed that the workpeople did their duty. The success of the firm could not have been attained without the help of the workmen, and therefore their interests were bound up together. As to the alteration of tile name of the firm, the name of Wm. Gossage and Sons had established itself as the premier firm in soap making in the world, and in his term it was never going to be altered. (Applause.)—Mr. F. H. Gossage also &livered a speech, in which he expressed the hope that the en- largement of the works would be for the benefit of the men and strongly advised the young people to take ad- vantage qf the technical instruction to be gained at the Science and Art classes.

div.head: THEATRICAL LICEMES AT WIDNES.
div.p: THEATRICAL LICEMES AT WIDNES.

A special sessien Was held at the Widnes Poliee Court,on Thursday, for the purpose of hearing appli- cations for theatrical licenses. The magistrates on the Bench were Messrs. 11. Wade-Deacon,H. Gaskell, jun., J. Birtlhall, and Stapleton Brotherton.—Mr. James Kiddie, lessee and manager of the Alexandra Theatre, applied for a renewal of the license to per- form stage plays in that building. He stated that the theatre was exactly in the same condition as last year, and the iron curtain was lowered and raised each night. The libense was renewed.—On behalf of Mr. Daniel Cohen, formerly manager of the Alexandra Theatre, Mr. Knowles, solicitor, applied for a theatrical license to a new building which had been erected in Widnes-road, adjoining the Grapes Hotel. It was a wooden structure with a canvas roof, with wooden supports. Mr. Sinclair, the surveyor to the Local Board, had inspected the building and he required cer- tain alterations and additions to be made, including the 'fixing of a hydrant and hose, and Mr. Cohen was wilting to carry out everything he desired. Smoking and drinking would not be allowed. The building would accommodate 1,100 people, and there were six exits, by means of which it could be cleared of a full audience in about a minute.—Mr. luig- ginson deposed to having prepared the plans of the building, which he said Was a much better structure than the Theatre Royal, which the Bench formerly licensed.—Mr. Cohen confirmed his advocate's state- ment, and said tie building had been licensed at Rugby and at Stratford-on-Avon. As the building was on the ground floor, an iron curtain would be of no use, and it could not be fixed up there.—By Mr. Swift (who opposed the application on behalf of the proprietors of the Alex- andra Theatre) : lie denied that he or the proprietors parted because they complained he had mismanaged the theatre. They parted because he would not allow one of the proprietors to interfere.—Mr. Swift: They com- plained the takings were coming down P—Witness : No. I made money every week. He added that takings al- ways came down in summer. Mr. Sinclair, sur- veyor to the Local Board, was called, and put in a report he had prepared, describing the building fully. If the alterations and additions he suggested .avere carried out, he considered it won/13 be a suitable building to be licensed.—By Mr. Swift: He should ob- ject to the building remaining in the town more than two years. Any fire on the stage would spread very quickly.—By Mr. Deacon: The building could be cleared in about a minute and-a-half.—RS. Laing said the Alex- andra Threate was very well conducted when Mr. Cohen was manager.—Mr. Swift :We admit that.—Mr. Swift then addressed the Bench, remarking that his clients were to some extent in a selfish position. They had erected a substantial building at a cost of £5OOO, and certain requirements of the magistrates had been car- ried out, including an iron curtain, which put the pro- prietors to a further expense of £l3O. If an iron curtain was necessary in a substantial brick building, he sub- mitted it was still more essential in a building of this description, which he contended should not be licensed by the Court without there was an overwhelming necessity for such a place. Up to Christmas the proprietors of the Alexandra Theatre were doing fairly well, the takings being about £lOO to £l2O a week; but since then they had diminished to about £5O a week, and the proprietors thought it necessary to part with Mr. Cohen. There was not room in the town for two buildings licensed for the performance of stage plays, and it would not be right or fair of the Bench to license a new theatre unless they felt it would supply a want on the part of thepublic.—Mr.Kiddiehaving given evidence, the Bench retired to consider the application, and on returning Mr. Deacon said they had carefully considered the,naatter, and had decided not to grant the license.

Lloyd's agent at Athenstelegraphed, on Thursday, that it is reported that the Austrian Lloyd steamer Berenice was in collision with a British steamer, Holway or Holiday, off Cerigo, and that the Berenice was beached. The passengers were landed at Syra.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.

BY AtS: OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. Widnesians are being at present agitated on the subject of the incorporation of the town. The Ratepayers Association and the local members of thedrisk National League are the principal advo- cates for such a course. and information is beim,b collected to show the advantage and benefit to be derived by the inhabitants if the town is converted into a municipality. The Town Clerk of Nelson, a recently formed borough, thus sums up the advantages in a letter to the secretary of the Widnes Ratepayers' Association —l, purer elections; 2, abolition of the property Qualifications of membership; 3, one man one vote; 4, increased status; 5, more local independence and lesa control by the Local Government Board; 6, the privilege of having the Mayor during his term of office, and for one year afterwards, as a justice of the peace; 7, the right to elect aldermen; 8, the govern, ing powers of the Council are more extensive, in,- eluding the privilege, if desired, of maintaining a borough police force; there can also be a separate commission of the peace {borough bench) appointed, by which means the borough will secure the tines, court fees, &c., for the borough funds; 9, the Coun- cil is generally trusted by Parliament with the con- trol of most of its functions, without so much control as is exercised by the Local Government Board over Local Boards. Local authorities naturally rebel at so much interference, and good men gradu- ally weary of taking part in performances when they are reduced to puppets." In this succient summary there is one omission; the Town Clerk has forgotten to state how much the rates of Nelson have increased since the con- version of that thriving town into a borough because an unvarying result of incorporation is an. increase in that respect. Considering the rapid growth of Widnes and the amount of money ex- pended on sewering, road making, hospitals, and other public works, the rates are at present very low as compared with the corporations in the locality. The best reasons for converting Widnes linto a municipality are those enumerated under 1,2, 3, and 5. The right to elect aldermen is more of a curse than a blessing in many instances, while the "increased status" may be allowed to pass as a little vanity. Speaking generally, however, the ratepayers would be better represented under a Corporation ; public improvements and undertak- ings could be more readily carried out ;. and the town altogether would occupy a more indepen- dent position;. hut at the same time, there can be no question that the town is admirably managed by ' our present Local Board with Mr. Gossage at their bead. It is probable that the question will be discussed at the next meeting of the Local Board, but it is very unlikely that any decision will then be arrived at. The Runcorn Musical Society have completed their arrangements for the forthcoming concert season, and the music loving public will be interes- ted in learning of the good things in store for them. Three concerts are to be given in the Drill Hall, Greenway-rd, The first, which is fixed to take place early in November, when the vocalists will be Madame Clara Samuells and Mr. Edward Grime. The orchestra, however, will occupy the greater por- tion of the evening by selections from "Dorothy " and" Faust," and solos by the principal instrumen- talists. On December 16th, Handel's " Messiah," with Mozart's accompaniments will be performed and the principals engaged are Miss Marianne Fenna, Miss Dews, Mr. Edwin Houghton, and Mr. Lucas Williams. The third and last concert is fixed for March 17th, 1891, when Mendelssohn's " Elijah " will be rendered. The chorus on the occasion will be Madame Conway, Miss Emilie Lloyd, Mr. Harry Guy, and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint.

div.head: ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, yesterday, a man who gave his name and address as Peter Rowe, 25, Liverpool-st., St. Helens. was charged with burglar- iously breaking and entering the Appleton Academy, where Mr. Robert Lowe, of Warrington, wa:FJ. ducting an auction sale, early tb I.C.2blft same morning. Superintendent t applied for a remand until to-nay (Saturday), which was granted.

div.head: MERSEY MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A MERSEY MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn Burial Board Office on Monday, on the body of a man unknown, which was picked up near Eastnam by a river packet and brought to Runcorn. The body was apparently that of a man about 50 years of age, five feet nine inches high, and was dressed in a blue ribbed suit, with Wm stockings and new lace-up boots. In a brown silk necktie was a gold horse shoe pin. The moustache anct beard of the deceased were turning from brown to grey,--A. verdict of "found dead" was returned.—The Coroner remarked that it was a pity the body had not been landed at Eastham.

IDENTITCATIoiI. Since the deceased 'as interred in the cemetery, it hag been ascertained that the body is that of John Bennett, of Liverpool, who was formerly manager of the Work- ingmen's Club, Church-st.,ltuncorn. As the body was buried in a pauper's grave, the friends of the deceased are anxious to have the remains interred in another part of the cemetery, and with proper ceremony, and it is stated that an application will be made to the Home Secretary on the subject. Although there were several jurymen who were well acquainted with the deceased, his features were so altered through long immersion in the water, that they did not recognise him.

FRODSHAM. OPEN AIR CONCERT.—The first of a series of open air , concerti; was given by the Frodsharn Military brass band, ably conducted by Mr. William Jones, the bandmaster, in the Main-street, on Saturday evening. The several items in the programme were thoroughly appreciated. PARISH CHURCH Cm:att.—The annual trip of the adult members of the choir took place on Monday, the place selected being Morecambe. Upwards of an hour was spent in looking at Lancaster Old Castle, Parish Church, &c. Morecambe wag' reached at 12.30, and the party at once sat down to a splendid dinner at the King's Arms Hotel. The afternoon was spent in various ways. BLAKE LEES CHAPEL, KINGSLEY. The anniversary services on behalf of the Sunday school were held in this chapel, on Sunday, the sermons being 'preached by Mr. J. Buckley, of Middlewich, afternoon and evening. Some assistance was given by the Runcorn Ellesmere-a. Chapel choir. The singing of the hymns, &c., was con- sidered to be quite satisfactory. The offertories for the day Amounted to over £l3. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—In connection with the Primi- tive Methodist Sunday School, the annual services were held in the Primitive Chapel, on Sunday, when the Rev. H. Davenport, circuit minister, preached morning and evening. In the afternoon a meeting was held for parents and friends, which was presided over by Mr. B. Parker, of Ilelsby. recitations being given by the scholars and addresses delivered by the Rev. J. D. Bray, pastor of Union Church, and the Rev. H. Davenport. Mr. James Hough presided at the organ throughout the several ser- vices. The special hymns were very well rendered by the choir and scholars. The collections realized over £lB.

REV. C. CLAY.—The Rev. C. Clay, pastor of the Congre- gational Church, left Lymm on Monday for a months' holidays. LONGEVITY AT WARMTH/TON.—Mr. Richard Ball, of Warburton, is now in his 91st year. He does a regular day's work as heartily as a man of 22. Mr. Ball has a son and two grandsons, who are tenant farmers under the Hon. Rowland E. Egerton-Warburton, who is him- , self 86 years of age. PRIMITIVE METIIODIST TEA MEETINTI.—The monthly tea meeting took place in the schoolroom, Eagle-brow, on Wednesday evening, the hostess being Mm. Edwards, Booth's-hill. There was a good attendance, and some useful work was doneln aid of a bazaar that is to be held in the hope of providing funds for the building:of a new chapel. PRIMROSE LE.tOITE.—A number of the members of the Lymm Habitation of the Primrose League proceeded by train to Sale Botanical Gardens last evening week, to take part in a joint demonstration of the Primrose Lea- gue Habitations of the Altrincham Division. Amongst those who journeyed from Lymm were Mr. and Mrs.T.P. Morris, Mr. E. A.Leigh, Mr.C. Maclver, Mr. D. Maclver, Captain Jones, Mr. A. W. Callendar, Mr. H. Greenall, and Mr. A. Watkin. CHOIR PICNIC TO CIIRSTER.-011 Wednesday the Wesleyan Chapel choir had a picnic to Chester. Leaving the village about seven o'clock in the morning, the party drove to Daresbury. Here fresh horses awaited them, and the journey was continued through Frodsham, Helsby and Dunham-o'th-Hill. Chester was reached at eleven o'clock. A very pleasant day was spent, and at seven o'clock a start homeward was made, Lymm being reached about eleven. The expenses incurred will be paid by friends in the congregation. SuccEssruz EERIIIITORS.—At the annual flower show held at Bowdon, on Saturday, the following Lymm ex- hibitors were successful in the classes mentioned :—Mrs. Grundy (Mr. Wm. Allman, gardener), Ist and 2nd for table decoration plants, Ist for nectarines, 2nd for goose- berries, 2nd for tomatoes, and Ist for Clibran's tomato. Mr. Win. Battersby, Lvinin Hall (gardener, Mr. F. Simp- son), obtained Ist and 2nd for table decoration plants, 2nd in 24 distinct varieties, single trusses, also 3rd in 6 varieties, 3rd for best six spikes of lilium, 3rd for best selection of fruit, 2nd for cherries, Ist for melons, let

for six dishes of vegetables, 3rd for cauliflowers, 3rd for tomatoes. DAMAGING A CANAL BOAT.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, a canal boatman named James Ainscott NUS summoned for damaging the boat Duchess Countess,,the property of the Ship Canal Company, on the 2Eth June. Mr. Neumann (of the firm of Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co.), appeared for the complain.. ants, and. Mr. A. E. Paterson for the defendant. From evidence which was adduced it appears that the defen- dant's boat on the day in question was proceeding along the. canal between Lymm and Oughtrington. The horse in drawing the boat pulled the rope over the complain- ant's flat and broke the chimney down, damage to the amount of ss. being done. The defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, 405., and ordered to pay the amount of the damage. ST. MARY'S PICNIC.—On Wednesday, the annual excur- sion of the Sunday school and congregation of the Parish Church took place in connection with St. George's, Altrincham to Blackpool. About 300 went from Lymrn,. accompanied by the C. E. Temperance Brass Band (under the conductorship of Mr. T. Gregson). in the afternoon tea was provided for the Sunday scholars at the Central Dining-rooms. After a most enjoyable day- the trains started for the homeward journey, but the engine attached to the second train, which cairied the- Lymm portion of the excursionists, came by an accident between Latchford and Thelwall, which detained them from a few minutes past nine till nearly 11.30. Many parents of the children were at the Lyrnm Station by nine o'clock, a few minutes after which the first train passed. Rain began to fall heavily,and when the second train did not come in, uneasiness gave place to excite- ment, as no information could be gathered from the officials. A few minutes after 11.30, however, the train, drew up.

div.head: IMPROVEMENT BILL.
div.p: THE IMPROVEMENT BILL.

The Warrington Extension, Water, and Imprc.ve- ment Bill passed the third reading in the House ot Commons last Tuesday,and will come before a Lords Committee next week. In all probability it will be unopposed. A special general meeting of the Warrington Water Works Company, convened in pursuance of the standing orders of the House of Lords tor the purpose of considering the Warrington Extension and Water Bill, 1890, on its introduction into that House, was held on Wednesday, in the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-st. Mr. J. Charlton Parr presided, in the absence of the chairman (Lord Winmarleigh) and deputy-chairman (Sir Gilbert Greeriall, Bart). A print of the Warrington Extension and Water Bill, 1890, was laid before the meeting, and at the re- quest of the chairman was read and explained 'by the law clerk. A. resolution in the fallowing terms was proposed by the chairman, seconded by Mr. R. Davies, and carried unanimously—viz. "That the Bill now read, intituled 'An Act to extend the boundaries of the borough of Warrington, to pro- vide for investing the undertaking of the Warring- ton Water Werks Company in the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington, and for other purposes, he, and the same is hereby, ap- proved of, subject to. such additions, alterations, and variations as Parliament may think fit to make therein." In conclusion, the chairman moved a vote of thanks to Mr. E. J. Nicholson, the company's law clerk, for his services in connection with the Bill. This was seconded by Mr. Wm. Sharp, and. carried unanimously.

div.head: COMING REVISION.-A FEW B INTS.
div.p: THE COMING REVISION.-A FEW B INTS.

The present is the -t-ii;e to prepare for the next general election, as the registration period is at hand. The next election will almost certainly be fought on the new register. The list of voters for 1891 will be published on Friday next,. August Ist, and be affixed to the door of every place of worship in the Borough, or can he aeon at the Liberal Club, Bewsey-st. Every Liberal who has been a house- holder for the twelve months eildi9v July 15th last, should examine the list for himself, and it hia name is omitted, or if there is any error, or misdescription of any kind, he should at once see Mr. Clayton, the Liberal agent, so that no vote may be lost for want of the necessary attention. Lodgers who occupy one or more rooms of the clear yearly value of .£lO are entitled to vote, and should claim iramediate.ly. Claim forms, and all other assistanoe, will be readily iurnished on application to Mr, Clayton, at the registration offices, Liberal Club. All claims must be served upon the overseers on or before August 200.

div.head: ACCIDENTS ON THE FAIR GROUND.
div.p: ACCIDENTS ON THE FAIR GROUND.

On Tuesday night, at ten o'clock, William Free- man, aged thirty, a warehouseman residing at 35, Nicholson-st., Warrington, got into one of the swingboats at the Warrington pleasure fair, along with another young man. The boat had not been long in motion, when, in mid air, it seemed to come in contact with the next boat. Freeman was thrown partly out of the boat, his legs becoming entangled alone preventing him from being precipitated to the ground. As it was he hung half way out, and on the boat descend- ing his head struck the ground, receiving a deep wound, and tearing Off a portion of the scalp. He was forcsd under the boat, and his right ear and eyebrow w6n Cut; while his right side was badly abraded. Freeman was taken to the Infirmary, where he got his wounds dressed, and although he had lost a considerable quantity of blood he was able to walk home. This was the ninth accident that had taken place inthe present fair, a little lad named James Jones also receiving painful injuries on Tuesday night. Two other accidents occurred at the fair ground on Wednesday evening. The most serious was one by which Mary Holliston, 18 years of age, residing at 4. Heaton-square, off Orford-st., sustained severe injuries to her head and back. She was swinging in one of the , boats, when she fell heavily to the ground. It was ' found that her injuries were serious and she was re- moved to the Infirmary in the police ambulance. Yesterday she was still in a dangerous condition. The second accident occurred to a lad named George Delooze, who resides with his parents in Mottram's yard. He was in the vicinity of the swings when one of the boats struck him violently on the tread and it was found neces- sary to remove him to the hospital.

div.head: TRAGEDY IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. INQUEST YESTERDAY.
div.p: THE TRAGEDY IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. INQUEST YESTERDAY.

Mr. Sidney Smelt, deputy coroner of Manchester, held an inquiry yesterday into the circumstances attending the death of John Clarkson, aged 27, manager of the Stanley Arms Inn, Broughton-road, Salford, who was found dead in a railway carriage on the arrival of a train from Liverpool at the Central Station, having evidently shot himself when journeying between Warrington and Manchester, under circumstances briefly referred to in another column.—Mr. Thomas Pike, of the St. Lake's Tavern, Salford, and °wiles of the Stanley Arms, said that he had that morning discovered a slight deficiency in the deceased's accounts. His accounts were straight three weeks ago, and witness did not think he intended to steal the money but to replace it. Deceased had been in his employ for nine years, and he would have trusted him to any extent. —Thomas Fletcher, foreman lainpman at the Centra Station, said that on the arrival of the train from Liver- pool at 3 15 p.m. on Thursday afternoon, he saw the de- ceased sitting in a first-class compartment with his head back and his mouth wide open. There were marks of blood at each corner of his mouth. Witness called to another porter and then entered the compartment. He found that deceased was dead, and at once informed the station master.—Detective-Sergeant Edwards deposed to finding a revolver in the carriage in which deceased travelled. It lay in his lap, as if it had fallen from his hand. Deceased was bleeding very much from the mouth, and witness at once had him removed to the Infirmary. It was there ascertained that the bullet had apparently passed out through the top of his head. The revolver was a five-chambered one ; four chambers were loaded, and one had been discharged. When searched deceased had in his possession £4 ss. qd., a gold watch and chain, and a small diamond pin. To all appearances deceased had shot himself, and there was nothing to suggest that any other person was concerned in his death.—Mr. Pike supplemented his evidehce by stating that deceased had for some time been under the impres- sion that he was going to win a large sum of money by backing horses, and he had at one time been very for tunate in that respect. But in Whit week he lost about £5O which he had previously won. On Wednesday he left home to go to Liverpool races, and witness thought he must have lost all that he had woa before. Witness had frequently cautioned deceased against the habit of betting. —The jury found that deceased committed suicide whilst insane.

UNDER THE SEAT: AN EXPENSIVE RIDE FROM WARRINGTON TO STOCNPORT. On Wednesday, at the Stockport Police Court, John Carr, a labourer, of no settled residence, was charged with travelling on the London and North- Western Railway without having previously paid his fare, and with intent to avoid payment, on July 23rd.—Thomas J. Slack, ticket collector at Edgeley Station, said that at 12.15 that morning he was examining tickets on the 10.45 train from Liver- pool, when, owing to what the guard told him he looked under one of the carriage seats and found the prisoner, who had no ticket. He said he was travelling from Warrington to Gateshead, and that. his ticket bad been taken from him.—A fine of 10s. and costs, or 14 days' hard labour, was imposed.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WIFE ASSAULT..

William Smith, a hawker, was brought before the ' Warrington magistrates on Thursday morning' on a charge of having assaulted his wife early the same morn- ing, in Hill-st. An officer said that prisoner knocked his wife down, and her screams could be heard "all over the town." The wife, however, said that he did not assault her, he only "chased" her because she had been having drink. It was all her own fault. The case was dismissed on the payment of the lock-up fee, one shilling.

A TEARFTIL PRISONER BEGS OFF. The tearful mood occasionally has its effect on the feelings of the magistrates. Those who sat at the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, had before them a young fellow named Martin Connolley, who was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Rose-yard, on Saturday night, and with having assaulted Constable Hampson. He protested that he was innocent, and was in some way or another the victim of circumstances, and as he was very tearful, the Bench took pity on him, and discharged him with a caution.

NEGLECT OF FAMILY. On Thursday, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named James Shaw was brought up in custody on a charge of having neglected his wife and two children, on the 23rd inst. Mr. Shearer, who proved the case, said that the prisoner's wife applied for relief, and he found her and the children in a destitute condition. There was no food in the house, and one of the children was absolutely naked. Since Walking Day he had only given his wife a few shillings. Prisoner asked for a chance, and promised not to offend again, but the mag- istrates thought he desecved punishment, and sent him to prison for a month. THE MUZZLING ORDER.

At the Warrington icsiii";-CO-ur-t,---o-n—Monday, James Strange was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled.—Constable 20 said that at about four o'clock on the morning of the 9th inst., he saw a brown retriever dog belonging to the defendant,unmuzzledjn the street.—Alderman Davies: Was he sober. (Laughter.) If the dog will promise not to do it again he may " retrieve" his character.—The defendant said that the dog was muzzled, and the Constable, asked why he did not take the dog to the-police station, said that he would not go near it, "for his own benefit."—The magistrates thought there was a doubt about the case, and dismissed it.

A CHARGE OF EMBEZZLEMENT DISMISSED. A rather curious case of alleged embezzlement was before Messrs. R. Garnett and W. Owen at the Warring- ton Police Court,on Tuesday. John Price, 58, Sharp-st., a carter in the employ of J. H. Fleming, jun., contrac- tor, was charged with embezzling 9s. ed., the money of his employer. Prosecutor said that in May last the defendant delivered a quantity of lime bottoms to a Mr. Owen in Bank-st. At the same time the bill was pre- sented, paid, and receipted, but the defendant had not paid the money over to him. Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared for the defendant, contended that the matter was purely one of account, as Mr. Fleming owed Price some money for wages due, and proceedings were pend- ing between them in another court. The magistrates dismissed the case, but considered the defendant had acted injudiciously in retaining the money so long. AN OLD OFFENDER'S ATTEMPT TO REFORM. Daniel Hennessey made his twenty-second appearance at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, having been booked for drunkenness and disorderly conduct. It appeared that the police were called to a row that was in progress at the house where the Hennessys live. Accord- ing to the Constable who proved the case, things must have been pretty lively, as " the furniture was broken, and meat was flying about the house." This, the Con- stable very rightly thought, was disgraceful, and as the prisoner was drunk, and was otherwise misbehaving himself, the officer locked him up. Prisoner, it was incidentally mentioned, seized his father by the throat, and addressed him as a "bald headed oh! Pri- soner now told the magistrates that he had been tryieg to reform as well as he could. He bad been work'ng bard every day, but I'..`.'.:;aiise Wante.A t'Z'reigett/21° 1111 l y interfered with him, as they wanted his money to spend in drink. The Bench, however, prob- ably thinking under the circumstances that Daniel's reformation was a good deal of a delusion, sent him to jail for a month. THE" BLACKEST SPOT" IN WADDINGTON. Inspector Norman, of the Warrington sanitary depart- I ment, drew a rather vivid picture at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, of what he termed one of the "blackest snots" in the town. A man named Joseph Varty, whose wife appeared, was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him' to abate a nuisance at 5, Croppers-brow. The house in question, Mr. Norman said, was a small one without ventilation. There was little br no furniture in it, and some straw formed all there was in the way of beds. He had seen some "black spots," but he never saw any- thing like this one. Everything in it was black; even the mother's eyes were black on the occasion of his visit. The house was " stewing in filth," and the floor looked as though a regiment might have walked over it. The wife of the defendant stated to the Bench that she had been ill, and had not been able to look after the house. The magistrates, at the request of Mr. Norman, made an order that the house should be closed, until it was cleansed and made habitable. Defendant was allowed until Thursday to obtain another house. A HORSE DEALER PROPERLY PUNISHED FOR ASSAULT. At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, a young man named Downes Varey, who described himself as a horse dealer from Leeds, was charged with violently assaulting his wife by striking and kicking her on the previous afternoon in Foundry-street; and also with assaulting Police Constables Bruen and David Jones. He was further charged with damaging P.C. Bruen's cape to the amount of 2s. 6&—P.C. Bruen said that about four o'clock on Friday afternoon he was on duty in Winwick-st. with Constable Jones. They heard screams proceeding from the direction of Foundry-st., and on going there saw the prisoner striking his wife with a whipstock. Ile knocked her down with a heavy blow en the head, which caused blood to flow freely. Whilst onthe ground he kicked her, and when witness interfered, the prisoner struck him a blow in the eye. With assistance the prisoner was taken into custody. He was very violent on the way to the police station, and several companions endeavoured to rescue him. Prisoner struck witness on the head, and kicked him about the legs. He tripped Constable Jones, and also knocked him down, and tore witness's cape. In answer to the Chief Constable, witness said that prisoner used all the violence he possibly could.—Corroborative evi- dence having been given, prisoner said he was very sorry for what he had done, and hoped the magistrates would let him off as lightly as they could.—The Chair- man: You did not spare your wife nor the police. I think the utmost penalty ought to be inflcted ; I think the case is a very aggravated one.—The Deputy Clerk (Mr. G. F. F. White) intimated that the prisoner had £l7 10s. on him when taken into custody, and after some consideration, the Bench decided to fine him £5 and costs for the assault upon his wife, and £5 and costs for assaulting the police, or in default of payment two months' imprisonment for each offence.—Prisoner: I am willing to pay the money.
MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROU(111 POLICE COURT.
SATIIRDAY.—Before Mr. Robert Garnett and Councillor
Voisey. DRIINICENNESS.—For being drunk and disorderly in Queen-st., on Friday night, John Fitzsimmons was fined ss. including Costs. MOND-IY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb),

Alderman Sutton and Aldertnan Davies. SLEEPING Cur.—Elizabeth Riley was charged with sleeping out in a yard in Wilson ratten-st., the same morning. She was dismissed on promising to leave the town. DEUNKENNESS.—Mary Dagnall, for having been drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., on the previous morning, was i sent to the workhouse.—Daniel Hennessy, charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Cropper's-brow, on the 13th ult., was sent to prison for a month. OBSTRUCTION.—Thomas Taylor, a farmer, was sum- moned for having caused an obstruction in Market-st.,by allowing his horse and cart to remain there for an un- reasonable length of time. He was ordered to pay the costs us. 61 Michael McDermot,charged with a similar offence, was also ordered to pay the costs. div.head: LORD WOLSELEY'S IRISH AGENT.
div.p: LORD WOLSELEY'S IRISH AGENT.

In Dublin, on Saturday, the Lord Chancellor of Ire- land struck of the rolls Of Irish solicitors the name of Mr. Abraham Betas, who was Lord Wolseley's Irish agent. Mr. Belas, who had an extensive practice, has absconded, and large defalcations have been discovered. The Lord Chancellor expressed great regret at having to perform so painful a duty.

div.p: EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF A.
POLICEMAN.

At Stafford on Thursday P.C. Goodman was fined £3 10i. and costs for an extraordinary assault. The officer rushed among a number of children who were cheering at a school treat, and knocked the little ones about severe- ly. The bystanders remonstrated. The constable then attacked three persons in the crowd with his staff, and split open a man's head. The magistrates expressed the opinion that Goodman was unfitted to be a police- man.
lilt. CHAMBERLAIN'S AMERICAN TOUR.

Mr. and Mrs. Chamberlain will leave England on the 6th of August for the United States. It is understood in Birmingham Liberal Unionist circles that the Right hon. gentleman has been entrusted with semi-diplomatic functions in connection with the Newfoundland and Pacific fisheries disputes, and that he will use his influ ence in high quarter for facilitating an understanding between England and America. The proposed garden party at Highbury on Saturday to the West Birmingham Liberal Uniunists has been postponed till August 2nd.

WARRINGTON (2NP) v. Si. HELRNS (2ND).—Played at St. Helens, on Saturday; and resulted in a very easy win for the visitors. Owing to the good bcwling of Bell, who took eight wickets for 23 runs, St. Helens could only compile 43 runs, Johnson and Ward being the only batsmen who could look at Bell. Howard kept wicket grandly for Warrington. On Warrington going in to bat, the first wicket fell at 14, and then Bell and Muir put on exactly 100 runs,before Muir fell to a catch. He had played on the whole very nice cricket, his defence play being very good. He was in eighty minutes for his 30. Brown made the fielders lively for a few minutes, and was then bowled with a very good ball. On Bulli- vant joining Bell, another long stand was made, 37 runs' being added before Bell was out, after a magnificent dis- play of good sound cricket. WAIIIIINGTON V. LIVERPOOL—The return fixture be- tween these clubs was played at Arpley on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of specta- tators. Warrington won the toss, and commenced bat- ting with Crosfield and Armstrong to the deliveries of A. G. Steel and Shoubridge. A poor stand was made, as Armstrong was caught before a run had been scored. With Crosfield and Smith together each opened with a four. Smith was very smartly taken in the slips for 10. Lawton got his leg before to Shoubridge before he had scored ; 2 and 3 wickets for 26. Two overs later Cros- field was given out same way; 4 for 31. Eight wickets had fallen for 37, when Voisey and Jolley made a most determined and useful stand, taking the score to 77 before they were parted. Captain Adam assisted to put on 14 for the last wicket, when Jolley was run out for an invaluable 35. Going in fifth at 32 he was last out, and had played good and patient cricket. His 35 included 4 fours, 1 three, and 3 twos. The visitors' fielding was very close. Liverpool, who opened with Porter and A. G. Steel to the deliveries of Adam and Jolley, started none too well, for at 9 Porter was caught for a single. Clarkson and Steel were putting runs together quickly, so Crosfield went on, vice Adam, at the railway end at 30, and in his fourth over Clarkson was bowled; 3 for 45. The next three wickets fell at 50. A. G. Steel was leg before for 34, made up of 4 fours, 2 threes, 2 twos, and singles. Nona of the Liverpool men could play the bowl- ing, except White. lie and Shoubridg,e looked like saving t the match but with a splendid ball Jolley beat the latter. div.head: FASTING MAN.
div.p: THE FASTING MAN.

Gout has manifested itself in Jacque's right hand, and in such a severe form that he was, on Tuesday, unable to continue the practice of signing his biographies. The pain also was so great in the night that his sleep was much curtailed. In other respects Jacques is in good condition. Up to Tuesday. when he completed the thirty-second day of his undertaking, he had lost 241 b. 9oz. in weight, or 41b. Boz. less than Succi did in the cor- responding portion of his forty days' fast. At ten on Tuesday night, ,Tacques had been without food for 774 hours.

div.head: MR. GLA.DSTONE- AND AMERICA.
div.p: MR. GLA.DSTONE- AND AMERICA.

Mr. Gladstone was presented in London, on Thursday, with a series of addresses adopted lately at a meeting held in New York under the presidency of General Sher- man. Not long ago Mr. Gladstone, in response to a request, sent a message through the phonograph to America pointing out the importance of thrift and self- help, and the resolutions adopted in acknowledgment of the message, testifying to the Liberal leader's qualities as a statesman, were also spoken into the phonograph. Colonel Gouraud now presented the addresses in an album and also the phonograph used to Mr. Gladstone, who in accepting the gift spoke of the high character of General Sherman and of the kindness he had ever received from the American people. These manifesta- tions touched him deeply and strengthened his kindly feelings towards America.

div.head: SUICIDE IN A MANCHESTER EXPRESS.
div.p: SUICIDE IN A MANCHESTER EXPRESS.

On Thursday afternoon, a youngman named Clark- son, said to have lived at Salford, was in a compart- ment of an express train from Liverpool to Manchester, when it made the usual stoppage at the Central Station at Warrington. He delivered up his ticket when the collector came round, but on the arrival of the train at Manchester the servants of the company found him to be dead and besmeared with blood. It was evidently a case of suicide, for a revolver lay besides the deceased, and an examina- tion showed that one of its five chambers had been recently discharged. The suiciflo had apparently put the weapon to his mouth, and the bullet had come out at the top of his head, and was found in the carriage. Deceased. who was very well dressed, had in his possession .£4 15s. in money, in addition to other articles. The body was conveyed from the station to the Infirmary Mortuary.

CRICKET.

Whatever may be the result of the Australian tour from a cricket point of view, there can be little doubt as to its success in a financial sense, as there have been good gates nearly everywhere they have gone.

Lancashire, notwithstanding the enforced absence of Briggs, gained two very creditable victories over Middle- sex and Yorkshire. On Saturday the match with Middlesex illustrated in a remarkable manner the vary- ing fortunes of the game, as, after twice appearing to hold a considerable advantage, the metropolitan county was in the end easily beaten. One of the features of the match was the excellent form displayed by three men whose play has hitherto been disappointing. Rawlin , had previously done nothing to justify his selection for Middlesex, yet in this match he scored 139 runs for once out, while Paul knd Yates won the game for Lancashire by putting on 136 runs together in the fourth innings, A great deal of the credit of Lancashire's single innings, victory over Yorkshire belongs to Mold and Watson,who bowled unchanged throughout the game, only Ulyett showing the least abilily to cope with them.

Dr. W. G. Grace, in "Forty Years' Cricket," gives the following resum6 of the important landmarks in the history of cricket : Club-ball was played in the 13th Century. Hand-in and Hand-out was played in 1477. The word 'Cricket' was used in 1550. Cat and Dog was played in Scotland in 1700. The oldest recorded match in existence is Kent V. England in 1746. The old Hambledon Club was formed in 1750, and con- tinued until the year 1791. Laws were in existence about the year 1700. The Marylebone C.C. was formed in 1787. The Gentlemen v. Players matches began in 1806. Round-arm bowling was in use in 1827. The I Zin,gari Club was formed in 1845. The All-England Eleven was formed in 1846. The United-England Eleven was formed in 1852. The first English team visited Canada and United States in 1861. The first English team visited Australia in 1862.

The match at Lord's between the cricket teams repre- senting England and Australia ended on Wednesday afternoon ma victory for the former by seven wickets. At Tunbridge Wells, Kent beat Middlesex by two wick- ets ; and at Birmingham Somersetshire defeated War- wickshire by 121 runs.

Lord Harris has lost no time in showing his cricketing form in India. He took part in a match between two local English teams at Poona, on the 26th ult., made 37 in the first innings, and carried his bat out with a fine score of 106 in the second. The noveland unprecedented spectacle of a Governor wielding the willow like an ordin- ary individual attracted a large crowd, and many of the native papers considered the event of sufficient Import- ance to comment upon it at some length.

CYCLING. At the Paddington Recreation Grounds, on Saturday, the second instalment of the National Cyclists' Union Championship was proceeded with. /n the final heat for the one mile safety bicycle championship, R. T. Meereely, Dublin University B.C.' won by three yards from H. H. Sanson, Catford C.C., Arthur du Cros being third; time, anin. 43 3-ssecs. The five miles amateur• bicycle championship went to F. T. Osmond, Brixton Ramblers 8.C., F. B. Wood, Brixton 8.C., and J. H. Adams, Lewisham and Catford C.C., being second and third re- spectively ; time, 14min. 34 4-ssecs. A big field went to the post for the 25 miles tricycle championship, which was won by L. Stroud, C.U.8.C., K. N. Stradmeki being second, and the French cyclist, E. Dervil, third; time, 1 hour 25min. 21 3-ssees,

At the Polytechnic lialTriT,Wsports, at Paddington, on Tuesday, W. Price won his heat in the two miles bicycle handicap from scratch in smin. 20 3-ssec., and after- wards won the final in the same time, beating Laurie's previous best of smin. 22 3-ssec. by 2sec. Price rode a safety, with pneumatic tyres. The record only stood a few minutes, however, as J. R. Mecredy shortly after- wards, with pacemakers, in a trial against the watch caused a sensation by reducing the record to smin. 15 1-ssec—the world's record for safeties, and only 3sec. slower than that for ordinaries.

A writer in the "Manchester Courier," in the course of an article dealing with "wheeling routes" in Cheshire, says that naturally enough the Chester road is first favourite among local cyclists, and few there are but sooner or later essay forth to cover the 40 miles that lie between the Mersey and the Dee. Most riders elect to go and return by the direct road, through Northwich and Delamere Forest, little suspecting that in so doing they only extract half the pleasure derivable from a jaunt to Chester and back. To make the out journey by Lymm and Frodsham is the way to total the sum. In so far as distance is concerned there is not a wide difference, nor is there much choice in the matter of road surface, for though this route is at times rough it never approaches the abominable state of read through Northwich ; it is true that there are many hills, but it is doubtful whether they exceed in number and steepness those of the more direct route. The advantage of change of route, there- fore,is at once apparent,while itt value is enhanced by a change in scenery equally fine, though of so totally different a character. When the rider's back is turned en smoky Warrington and the Ship Canal, the heights of verton soon come upon the view, and then, when Frods- ham is passed, a fine run under the frowning brow of Helsby Hill follows, coupled with a long stretching view of the silvery estuary of the Mersey on right, while far beyond extend the Clwyddian heights of Cambria.

div.head: BOWLS.
div.p: BOWLS.

This popular summer pastime is in full swing just now, and since the weather has altered for the better the local greens have been rather busy. It may not be aenerally known that the gatne is one of the oldest of English pastimes, its origin being traceable as far back as to the twelfth century. The word "howls." how- ever, occurs for the first time in 3 Henry VIII., cap, 3., where the game is defined as an unlawful pursuit, those who practised it at one time being liable to arrest. This order of things changed, fortunately for bowlers, and at the beginning of the eighteenth century no country mansion was considered complete without a bowling green.
