ST. HELENS LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
ACCESSION TO THE RANKS.

Mr. Samuel Taylor, barrister-at-law, 3, Dr. Johnson's- buildings, Temple, E.C., lord of the manor of Eccleston, near St. Helens, a descendant of an old Lancashire Con- servative family, has just become a member of the St. Helens Association of Gladstonian Liberals. We are in- formed that a few months ago Mr. Taylor, who was a member of the Newton Conservative Association, inti- mated that he could no longer tollow thepresent Govern- ment in their Irish policy, and that his sympathies lay with the followers of Mr. Gladstone in this important point. He therefore severed his connection with the Conservatives, and joined the Liberal Association of the division. Part of the Eccleston estates lie within the borough of St.Helens, and Mr. Taylor has felt it his duty to also join the Liberal Association of the borough. A few days since he paid his subscription to Councillor John Forster, chairman of the Executive Committee, and expressed the pleasure it would afford him to assist in the work of the association. Mr. Taylor may be ex- pected on the platform in support of Mr. W. R. Ken- nedy, Q.C., the Liberal candidate. The following shows how the estates came into the possession of the Taylor family :—Baines' History of Lancashire states : " Eccleston was part of the ancient barony of Widnes, and was held of the Earl of Ferrers by William de Deresbury in Sutton and Accliston, whose daughter Margery, about 1291, conveyed the manor of Eccleston to Henry he Noreis in marriage. In the reign of Edward 111. William he Norreys performed suit and service to the county, and wapentake for the manors of Sutton, Eccleston, and Rainhill, by the hands of Alan do Eccleston, his tenant. The pedigree of the Eccleston's ascends to Hugh, the grandfather of Robert, who lived in the time of Henry 111. ; Ralph Eccleston, in 14 Henry VIII. (1522) held the manors of Eccleston and Ravnel, which were extended to six caracutes of land,worth-L2O, by the service of half a knight's fee and a rent of ss. id. About 1567 Eccleston Hall was built. By an ordinance of Parliament the estates of Thomas Eccleston, of Eccles- ton, Esq., deceased, were sequestered in 1645, one fifth being allowed to his widow and children for their maintenance. The family were subsequently re-possessed of the estates, which descended to the late Thomas Eccleston, Esq., afterwards Scarisbrick of Scarisbrick, who sold Eccleston, about 1811, to Colonel Samuel Tay- lor, of Moston." The record is brought down in "The County families of the United Kingdom" (by Edward Watford, M.A.) as follows—" Samuel Taylor, Esq., of Eccleston Hall, Lancashire, eldest son of the late Colonel Samuel Taylor, of Moston, county Lancaster, by Hannah, daughter of William Hutchinson, Esq., of Bury, county Lancaster, born 1801, succeeded to estateslB2o, married 1825 Mary Ann, daughter of the Rev. John Still, Pre- bendary of Sarum, and has issue: Samuel, a magistrate for counties Lancaster and Westmoreland, born 1826; married 1858 Maria, daughter of the Rev. Iston Fell, of Amblesidet and has issue two sons and a daughter [the eldest son is the Mr. Samuel Taylor referred to political- ly in this notice]. This family has resided at Moston, near Manchester, and possessed property there since the fourteenth century. The grandfather of the present riroprietor was a merchant in Manchester."

div.head: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF ' WIDNES,
div.p: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF ' WIDNES,

Public opinion in Widnes will before long, it is expected, be called upon to decide whether it is, or is not, expedient to empower the local authority to apply bra charter of incorporation :for the town- ship. Already some steps have been taken by one or two representative bodies, in order that the f eel- ing of the ratepayers on this subject might be ascer- tained, and so far as can be judged the popular voice will almost unanimously be in favour of the proposed change. The Widnes Ratepayers' Associa- tion has discussed the subject at several of its recent meetings, and this association will receive the support of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League, for both bodies are heartily in unison as to the benefits which would result to the district if a charter of incorporation was granted. The township of Widnes comprises an extensive district of over 5,900 acres, and includes within its boundaries Appleton, Upton, and Farnworth. The Local Board was constituted in 1885, when the population was about 10,000, and the ratable value over £30,000. The district is now one of the most important centres of the chemical indust, is in the country; and the number of works and houses built of recent years has been wonderful. The population is now estimated to be about 31,000. When the census of 1881 was taken the figures were 24,918,but a special census was taken in 1888 for County Council purposes, and in that year thd population was found to be 29,723. We shall therefore be within the mark in placing the present population at about 31,000. The ratable value of the township has increased at an even greater ratio. From the return in the possession of the Local Board it will be seen that the figures under this head had rison to no less than £132,885 in 1890. No one can therefore accuse the residents of such an import- ant and rising centre of industry of being premature in seeking to obtain those more extended privileges which will be exercised by the members of the proposed Town Council of Widnes. Those corporate privileges which are now in possession of towns whose population and area rank below those of Widnes might be obtained without any difficulty by this township, if the ratepayers are unanimous. . - -

..... The advantages which are to be derived from the change are held to b 3 so obvious that it is a matter of surprise to these who know the district that the applica- tion has not been made long ago. From a ratepayer's point of view alone it is represented that the most im- portant of these are :—First, that in voting power every man who is a householder will be equal, whether he be an owner or an occupier ; secondly, the property quali- fication for membership of the governing body will be abolished ; and thirdly, the ejections generally will be carried out on a fairer and more satisfactory manner than is possible under the system which prevails in local board districts. It might seem at the first glance that the second of these advantages would prove of doubtful value. By the insertion of the property qualification for membership of a local board, men of standing in the district can alone find a place in the governingbody, and the ratepayers have not always an opportunity of send- ing from amongst their own body menbers who wlil look more particularly to their wishes. Theabolition of the: property qualification therefore throws open to any ratepayer the door of the Council chamber, but as the whole matter is in the hands of the ratepayers, it may safely be argued that the liberty thus granted is more likely to be used A.s in other places, for ,the good of the general body, than otherwise. Little need be said of the palpable benefits which are certain to result from the change in the system of election. Such a change is ad- mitted on all sides would be for the better. Again, the incorporation of the township is regarded as desirable from abother point of view. Local Boards are trio. great extent hampered (sometimes wisely it may be) by the constant intervention of the Local Government Board. Some such body, is, of course, under certain circumstances, necessary for the good government of localities, but this supervision and guidance should only be exercised within well defined limits, and the general opinion of competent judges, and the experience of the working of the Municipal Corporation Acts is held to prove that Town Councils have used their extended powers for the good of the districts over which they are set to govern. It must naturally be expected that. gentlemen who reside in a town know the wants of their neighbourhood much better than a Board in London, and they naturally enough wish to have powerto legislate for their own particular districts with as free a hand as pos- sible. The irksomeness of a position en a Local Board can only be properly appreciated by gentlemen who have been accustomed to the greater freedom of a Town Council. Further, the cast of governing a district under a Town Council is not materially increased, and in those districts where the expenditure has risen considerably those con- cerned are of opinion that the increased privileges, the better government,and the higher status of a council were in themselves an adequate return for the outlay. One direction in which a council has been sometimes regarded as proving a distinct advantage over a local board is in the greater facility with which its borrowing powers can be utilized : and here also a council can usually obtain

better financial Widnes was incorporated the town would naturally be divided into wards, and this would have the effect of simplifying elections. The accounts of the Corporation would also be kept under an improved system, and many minor changes would take place which it is believed would generally have the effect of improving the town in every respect. The advan- tages which would be derived from the incorporation of Widnes are therefore regarded as many and of great im- portance, while there is scarcely one argument advanced in favour of retaining there the present mode of local government. No shadow of complaint has been made against the present working of the Board, which under the conditions has done its work well ; but it ft felt by all who have studied this question that the contemplated change, if effected would be for the general advantage of the ratepayers of Widnes, '

div.head: ROYAL M. L AND N. L. SHOW.
div.p: THE ROYAL M. L AND N. L. SHOW.

The Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society's show, which for this year combines that of the Cheshire Agricultural Society, opened on Thursday morning in fine, dry, and breezy weather at Crewe. The total entrance list, numbering 3,451, is about a thousand in excess of last year's show at :Wigan, and also larger than for one or two years Ireviously. Horses are a very fair show, but dogs and poultry are somewhat deficient in numbers, and the police restrictions in regard to cattle have acted somewhat repressively on the entrance list in one or two classes. Of the live stock awards so far made Lord Crewe has secured first place in the short horn bull class for landlord's bull, and Sir Humphreys de Trafford in the two year old bull class.

ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES AT RUN- CORN GUARDIANS ELECTION. In the House of Commons, on Wednesday evening, Mr. Brunner (Northwich) gave notice to interrogate the PresideM of the Local Government Board, with reference to the irregularities at the late election of guardians of the poor for the township of Runcorn, whether he his aware that the clerk's office is at Frodsham, so that qualified electors who may not receive voting papers have either to walk eight miles or make a railway journey to obtain them ; whether he is also aware that the counting of the votes takes place at Dutton Workhouse, which is still further from Runcorn, and not accessible by railway, so that it is practically impossible for any- one neglected by the distributor or collector of voting papers to record his vote; and whether in view of the fact that the township of Runcorn con- tains more than half the population of the union, and that contested elections in the other townships are almost unknown, he will direct that voting papers should be procurable at the overseer's town- ship office at Runcorn, and that the counting of the votes should take place there.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED,
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED,
ISSUE OF NEW SHARES.

An extraordinary general meeting of the share- holders of this company was held yesterday after- noon, at the bank premises in Winwick-st., War- ' rington for the purpose of sanctioning the declara- tion of an interim diVidend, considering special resolutions of the directors proposing an increase of the capital of the company, and transacting general business. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Charlton Parr, chairman of the Board of Directors, and the other directors present wesa Colonel Gamble (St. Helens), Mr. P. Stubs (Warring- ton), Mr. E. Greenall ',Grappenhall), Colonel Mc- ._ . . .

Corquodale (Newton), Mr. -S. Turner (Aigburth), Mr. H. W. Meade-King (West Derby), and Mr. Cecil P. Parr (Ncrthwich). Among the shareholders present were, Captain Withington, Major Pickmere and Messrs. It. Pierpoint, Starkey Smith, J. D. Buckton, J. Rylands, R. Davies, 11. Greenall, W. Owen, A. Jolley, &c.

div.head: REPORT OF TUE DIRECTORS.
div.p: REPORT OF TUE DIRECTORS.

The directors reported that the profits of the half-year had been satisfactory, and they recommended that there be now declared, for the half-year ending 30th June, an interim dividend at the rate of 18 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, and payable on and after 29th July. After providing for this dividend, there remained a con- siderable balance, which was carried forward to the next account. The position and prospects of the Bank continued to be in every way satis- factory. A branch of the Bank had been open at Bolton and sub-branches at Golborne, Wrexham, and Ellesmere Port. As would be seen by notices that had been given of special resolutions to be submitted to the meeting, the directors proposed to issue propor- tionately to the shareholders on the register on that date 2,000 new shares at the price of £5O per share, of which £2O per share should be paid as capital, and £3O per share as premium. This issue, at a price so much below the market value of theshares, would be equivalent to a substantial bonus to the shareholders, it would add £40,000 to the paid up capital, making it £BOO,OOO, and £60,000 to the reserve fund, making it £360,000. The increased business of the bank enabled the directors to find employment for this addition of £lOO,OOO to the working capital.—The Chairman, in proposing the adoption of the report, referred to the special resolutions that the meeting would be asked to pass. The first resolution, that the nominal capital of the company should be increased, was so manifestly advantageous to the bank and the shareholders that it would require no recommendation to ensure its adoption. A second proposal, to the effect that the qualification of every director should be the holding iu his own right of 30 shares of the company, was made in consequence of a recognised inconvenience that had grown up, partly threugh the prosperity of the bank, but one which nevertheless might act prejudicially to its interests. The present minimum of shares to be held by a director was a hundred. He might remark, though he believed it to be quite unnecessary, that the directors made a pro- posal, not from any personal or individual feeling, or to meet any personal or individual case, but for the con- venience and advantage of the bank generally. Whenl the bank first started the shares were then £lO paid up, and the qualification was fixed at 100 shares, which meant £l,OOO. Since then, partly in consequence of another £lO being called up, but much more in conse- quence of the high premium at which the shares were quoted, that qualification of 100 shares had risen from £l,OOO to £B,OOO, and before any gentleman could be asked to join the board of directors, he must not only find £B,OOO, but must also obtain 100 shares. This was a difficulty and a disatility, and they thought it best to , ask for the alteration rather than legislate with any par- ticular caso in view.—Mr. EDWARD GREENALL seconded the adoption of the report, which, on it being explained , that that did not affect the two special resolutions re- . I ferred to, was unanimously agreed to.

div.head: DIVIDEND.
div.p: THE DIVIDEND.

Colonel GAMBLE proposed the declaration of an interim dividend at the rate of eighteen per cent., which, he said, was a larger dividend than they had hitherto had. How- ever, it certainly was not more than the state of the business justified.—Mr. John Rylands seconded the pro- posal, which was carried. THE SPECIAL RESOLUTIONS.

div.head: CHAIRMAN . proposed that the nominal capital of
div.p: The CHAIRMAN . proposed that the nominal capital of

the Company slioulCl be increased from £2,800,000, its present amount, to £3,000,000, by the creation of 2,000 new shares of LlOO each, such shares to be issued at the price of £5O per share. The prcpositiou was seconded without comment, on the motion of Captain Wi thi ngton. —Some discussion followed with regard to the second resolution,as to the qualification of directors being reduced from the holding of 100 share to 30shares,which was proposed by the CHAIRMAN, and seconded by Mr. R. PIERPOINT. The latter said that they all had faith in the directors, but he hoped that if the resolution was carried the new privilege would be made the exception and not the rule, as in a concern like that they wanted as directors substantial men, such as those who now formed the Board.—Mr. Joins Rmonos said he knew that the company was strong enough to do anything, but he thought that they should set a good example to limited companies generally. He thought that the proposed re- duction was going too far, and proposed as an amend- ment that the qualification be reduced to lay instead of to thirty shares.—Dr. BEAMEN seconded the amendment. —The CIIAIRMAN said that the directors had no strong feeling on the matter, and only wished to carry out the desires of the shareholders. They were anxious to have very substantial men as directors, but he might say that it was not always a monetary consideration that made the best director.—On the matter being put to the vote, I the original proposition was carried by an overwhelming Mak). Ity. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.head: TIT-BITS. A DERBYSHIRE TALE.
div.p: TIT-BITS. A DERBYSHIRE TALE.

-- About Wenty or thirty years since, a gentleman named Webster, who lived in the Woodlands, a wild uncultivated barren range of hills in Derbyshire. bordering upon the confines of Yorkshire, had occa- sion to go from home. The family, besides himself. consisted of the servant man, a young girl, and the housekeeper. At his departure he gave his man a strict charge to remain in the house along with the females, and not any account to absent himself at night, until his return. This the man promised to, do, and Mr. Webster proceeded on his lourney. At night, however, the man went out, notwithstanding all the earnest entreaties and remonstrances of the housekeeper to the contrary, and not coming in, she and the servant girl at the usual time went to bed. Some time in the night,. they were awakened by a loud knocking at. the door. The housekeeper get up, went down- stairs, and inquired who was there, and what wagc their business. She was informed that a friend of Mr. Webster being benighted, and the night wet and stormy, requested a night's lodging. She forthwith gave him admittance, rousedup the fire, led his horse, into the stable, and then returned to provide some- thing to eat for her guest, of which he partook, and was then shown to his chamber. On returning W' the kitchen, she took up his great coat in order to- dry it, when perceiving it to be, as she thought, very heavy, curiosity prompted her to examine - the pockets, in which she found a brace of • loaded pistols, and their own large carving knife Thunderstruck by this discovery, she imme- diately perceived what sort of a guest she bad. to deal with, and his intentions. However,. summoning up all her courage and resolution, she. proceeded softly up stairs, and, with a rope, fas— tened, as well as she could, the door of the room which the villain was; then went down, and in great perturbation of mind awaited the event. Shortly after a man came to the window, and in s- low, but distinct tone of voice, said, Are YOU ready ?" She grasped one of the pistols with a desperate resolution—presented it to his face—and fired I The report of the pistol alarmed the villain above, who attempted to get out of the room, hut, was stayed in his purpose by her saying, " if you open the door, you are a dead man."' She- then sent the servant girl for assistance, while tbe- remained, with the other pistol in her hand, guard- , jug the chamber door. When help arrived, that ; villain was taken into custody; and, on searching ; without, they found the seivant man shot dead. Another villain who was taken shortly after, met. ' with his deserts; and the housekeeper, who bad acted with such fidelity and such unparalleled Intrepidity, was soon after united to Mr. Webster.

div.head: WILLIE COSSAR PINS.
div.p: WILLIE COSSAR PINS.

'The large pins which the common people used denominate Willie Cossars, were formerly calleo boa; preens, on account of their price, only four or them being given by the chapman tor a halfpennY• The change of their name is said in the south country to have been occasioned by a remarkable circumstance. There was once a wandering macl- man, named Willie Cos.sar, who bore a terrible character everywhere for his rabid disposition.. This personage one day walking along an unfre- quented road, met a poor woman who did not know his person. He asked her if she were not afraid to walk abroad by herself, considering the numerous dangers which beset solitary, and especially female travellers. She answered that she never dreaded anything in her journeys, except the chance of en- countering a wild man of the name of Willie Coos:. Willie was so enraged at this, that, out of revenge* he picked out her eyes with a large bocile Pi That species of pins thenceforward received his name.

div.head: MINISTER AND THE COLLIERS.
div.p: THE MINISTER AND THE COLLIERS.

A Fife clergyman, of very gentle disposition, one Sunday came upon a pair of Borrowstownness col- liers, who had come over the Frith of Forth, and made a piratical descent upon one of his bean- fields. Disposed to take pacific measures with the offenders, the worthy man began to represent to them, in the first place, the sin of thus violating the sanctity of the Sabbath; in the second, the wicked" ness of destroying so much of his property while in an unripe state, and when it could be of so little service to themselves. " Stay," he entreated, "till the beans are ripe, and if you will not steal all' before that time, I shall willingly give you a whole peck as a sort of reward for your patience and honesty." "A deck 1" cried one of the wretches, in a tone of mingled astonishment and scorn; "a peck! gae wa', man, we vvadna tak your WI (boll) I"

div.head: TWO STORY-TELLERS.
div.p: THE TWO STORY-TELLERS.

The clergymen of two adjoining parishes in FOr. farshire (about the end of the last century) were both alike remarkable for an infinite fund of sneer dote, as well as for a prodigious willingness, or rather eagerness, to disclose it. When one of there • happened to be present in any company, be generally monopolised, or rather prevented, all 000' versatton; when both were present, there was constant and keenly-contested struggle for the first place. It fell out, on a certain morning, that , they breakfasted together, without any other company • when the host, having a kind of right of precedence in virtue of his place, commenced an excellent but very long-winded story, which bi? guest was compelled to listen to, though disposet at the end of every sentence, to strike in his parallel, and far more interesting tale. As the host proceeded with his story, he poured hot water Into the teapot; and so completely was he absorbed in-the interest of what he w.is relating, or rather_ perhaps so intent was he to engago the attention or his listener, that he took no auto of what be wee doing, but permitted the water first to overflow the vessel into which be was pouring it, then the table, and finally the floor. The guest observed what was going on; but, being resolved for once to eve his rival ample scope and verge enough* never indicated by word, or look, or gesture, tilet he perceived it, till at last, as the speaker brough' his voiceto a cadence, for the purpose of finishing the tale, he quietly remarked, "Aye, ye may BOP noo—it 's running out at the door 1"

div.head: TEE HYPOCHONDRIAC PRINCE
div.p: TEE HYPOCHONDRIAC PRINCE

Many distinguished persons, from a disease in the Imagination, have fallen into strange notions egard' lug their personal identity and character. In the memoirs of Count de Maurepas, there is an account given of a most singular hypochondriac in the person of the Prince of Bourbon. He once imagined bili self to be a bare, and would suffer no bell to be rur,l_e In the palace, lest the noise should scare him in ru'e woods. At another time he fancied himself to be 3 plant, and as he stood in the garden, insisted e,r) being watered. He some time afterwards imagine" he was dead, and refused all nourishment, for which, be said, he had no further occasion. This last whir° would have proved fatal, if his friends had not CO trived to disguise two persons, who were introdtice to him as his grandfather and Marshal L'Ll- embourg, and who, after some conversation 0011" ceming the shades, invited him to dine with Mar" shal Turenne. Our hypochondriac followed there' into a cellar prepared for the purpose, where be made a hearty meal. While this turn of his dot order prevailed, he always dined in the cellar wit". some noble ghost. It is somewhat remarkable tha.o this strange fantasy did not incapacitate him for buel: ne,ss, especially where his immediate interests weer: concerned. Hypochondriasm is doubtless proda In a great measure, from deep study, or from 03.: artificial mode of living, and a want of proper air anno exercise. We seldom hear of a ploughman or ta industrious artizan falling into that diseased era'; of the imagination, and considering thernseive , hares, vegetables, plants, or disembodied spirirS•

div.head: SHOOTING AT BISLEY.
div.p: THE SHOOTING AT BISLEY.

--- Saturday was an extremely heavy day at Bisley. Not I 'only had the second stage of the Queen's and other im- portant events to be decided, but ties had also to be shot off in. the first stage of the Queen's, in the S. George's,and hi "The Graphie competitions, During the earlier part of the day the weather was as bad as it could be from the marksman's point of view. A close contest took place at the final range of the Queen's Second Stage for the Silver Medal, which at length fell to Private Murray, 3rd V.B. Gordon Highlanders, with an aggregate score of 204. Private Taylor, 2nd V.B. North , •Staffordshire, was second with 203. In shooting the ties for the Bronze Medal, Private McLachlan, Bth Lanark, made three bullseyes and won. Captain Gibbs, Bristol Engineers, won the St. George's Vase. Sergeant Reid, td V.B. Gordon Highlanders, won" The Graphic" Cup. On Monday the most important competition 'decided was that for the National ' Challenge Trophy, which is ao_ntested annually by England, Scotland, Ireland, and ,wales, one team of twenty from each country.. Scotland led at the three ranges closely followed by England, Wales standing third at the first and second ranges. Scotland won with 1,817 points, England following with 1,808, Ireland 1,763, and Wales 1,758. On Wednesday there were several miscellaneous Zulpetitions. Captain Gibbs, of Bristol, won the 'Juke of Cambridge's Prize; Mr. Braithwaite, of the Irish eight, took the Albert Jewel; the English tr,eatil made the highest score, 704, for the Kolapore ..",1113; and the Volunteers the highest score, 695, for the United Service Challenge Cup. WINNER OF .THE QUEEN'S PRIZE. The great event of the Sisley meeting was decided on Tuesday, and Sergeant Bates, of the Ist Warwick, is Queen's prizernan of 18 90 with a grand aggregate of 278 Points. Sergeant Bates has been a volunteer since 1867. Ming in that year, he in 1868 fired his first shot at imbledon, and was then fortunate enough to be includ- •ed in the last 60 who fired in the Queen's. This was no 'mean distinction for a recruit. Since 1868 he has been • a regular attendant at the meetings of the National Rifle Association, and the present is the seventh occasion up- on which he has shot in the final stage. At one pre- vic'us meeting he in the Queen's ran up an aggregate 'which gave him seventh place, but that was his great- '„est achievement with the rifle in the premeir competition. in 1888 Sergeant Bates went as the representative of England to the great American Rifle contest at Creed. flora, and for several successive years he has shot in the English team at the Wimbledon butts. Sergeant Bates is a resident of Birmingham' in which city are the headquarters of his battalion. He is by occupation a flunfitter, is just short af 50 years of age, and has sev- eral grandchildren. A comparison between this and rest • Year's firing in the final stage of the Queen's shows that in ~.1889 the gold medal was won by Sergeant Reid, of the Ist !,-.,,Anark Engineers, with a total of 281 marks, being ;dime points above the grand aggregate of this year. major Pearse, of the 40th V.B. Devon, then came within • one mark of the champion. but this year Sergeant Bates' eecond, Private Murray, 3rd Gordon Highlanders, is 'eight points behind him. In this fact lies the reason Ahy the final stage proved a less exciting event than it Was at the last °Wimbledon meeting. Sergeant Bates having obtained the lead kept it, so that there was no luch varying fortune as left the issue of the day depen- dent upon a single mark, but in the result it was a highly 'Popular victory, for no winner of the Queen's trophy 1:1)79.8 ever feted in more ungrudging style, not exclusively .1 9 the great assemblage of the public at the firing points, but by those who had fought him shot for shot through -all the three stages. The firing in the 800 yards began at half-past two ,o'clock on the long range butts on the side of the Clock Tower Hill, opposite to the targets at which the two earlier stages were contested. The new position is per- naps less favourable for high scoring, as the ground is more exposed, and this afternoon the full force of a stiff south-west breeze was felt at the firing points while the Marksmen were firing at both the 800 and 900 yards dis- tacce. The public crowded at the ropes, and almost quadrupled in numbers by the time the 900 yards firing as opened, so that some thousands were present, and aniong them were many ladies, who occupied chairs Munediately to the rear of the marksmen. The event was shot off more briskly than was anticipated, and was flished at 5.20. Below are the full aggregates :- Ist 2nd 3rd Btge. Btge. Btge. Ttl. 800 900

Considerable local interest has been manifested in the Shooting of the St. Helens Volunteers, who have taken Part in the great volunteer contests at Sisley. Up to Tuesday the winnings of the St. Helens men amounted to 2118 or £l2O, with four badges and four jewels. This is about the same as was won last year. This year the local men had a run of bad luck in the contest for the Queen's prize, but in tho ether competitions they have shot well all round. Sergeant West's score made in the first stage of the Queen's was the lowest he has Made for ten years, and it is many years since the 2nd V.B. had no representative in the Queen's hundred. Last Year there were two, the year previous three, and the Year before that five. Only three of the St. Helens men reached the second stage, Corporal Taylor, Private McGill and Sergeant Wilson, who had scores of 93, 91, ftud 89 respectively. In the second! stage ;McGill and Wilson each scored 94, while Taylor was 9 points lower, the totals being McGill 185 ; Wilson 183 ; and Taylor 438- McGill and Wilson win prizes of £4 each and Tay- lor a prize of £3. THE EDUCATION CODE NEW MINUTE.

A new minute amending the Education Code has been issued. The principal changes are these—children who have passed in the seventh standard may remain in school until they are 14 years of age, and have their at- tendances counted for grants. The regulations in the matter of untrained teachers are not to be retrospective. School accounts and reports may be inspected by rate- payers " in any convenient place," and not necessarily in the schoolroom. A failure in recitation is not to pre- vent a child from entering the next year for special sub- jects. Small rural schools of not more than 20 in attend- ance may have a female teacher instead of a pupil teacher ; the Department is not to have the option of making the £lO extra grants in these small schools any less sum than £lO. Girls in every school who are ex- amined in special subjects onlY (though holding a high standard certificate) may earn the 2s. cooking grant. The extra .210 given to schools when the population is not more than 500, is not to be subject to the 17s. 6d limit. July, instead of December, is fixed for the Day Training College examinations, to accommodate the courses of in- struction with those of the Universities with which the Training Colleges will be associated.

div.head: TWO TRAGEDIES IN GLASGOW.
div.p: TWO TRAGEDIES IN GLASGOW.

With the beginning of the Glasgow Fair holiday, a shocking tragedy occurred in the Saltmarket on Satur- day morning. Two policemen were summoned to a lodging-house in that street, and on entering they found the proprietor, Thomas Kane, lying dead. He had been deeply stabbed on the right breast, and his head was dreadfully hacked, there being no fewer than 12 wounds on that part. The body, which was warm was removed to the police station mortuary. A quarrel had taken place between deceased and Thomas M'Gribben, a cripple, aud it is alleged that M'Gribben stabbed Kane. Both men were under the influence of liquor. M'Gribben was apprehended. A man niniedjohn M'lnnes, a slipper maker, 46 years of age, is in custody in Glasgow on a charge of having murdered a woman named Catherine M‘Lachlan, with whom he cohabited. The woman is respectably con- nected, but during the ten years of her connection with M'lnnes they lived a miserable, dissolute life. On Satur- day afternoon they had been together at the shows at Vinegar Hill, and the woman returned about eleven o'clock. About half-past eleven M'lnnes went to the house of his mother, and told her that Kate was drunk, and that he had given her a good thrashing. The mother went to the house, and found the woman lying in the bed recess. She spoke to her, but got no answer, and left the house. About six o'clock in the morning M'lnnes gave information at the Eastern police office that his wife had died during the night. He was detained in custody, and on the house being examined the woman was found lying in the bed recess, the apartment being absolutely destitute of furniture. The body was quite cold, and she had evidently been for some time dead.
WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT WIDNES. "A" COMPANY PRIZE COMPETITION.

The musketry parts of this competition took place on Saturday at Widnes. The competition was for a large silver challenge cup, presented to the company by Major Pickmere, together with five money prizes of 155., 125., 10s., Bs., and 6s. respectively, given by Mr. J. It. Buckton, Major Litton, and Mr. H. Greenall. It consists of three stages, the first being points allowed for attendance at drills during the drill season, but prior to the inspection. The second stage is for firing five rounds at 400 yards, five at 500 , yards, and ten at 600 yards, all lying down, being the ' same as the regulation second class firing. The third stage consists of individual range defence practice, wherein each man fires one round at every 30 paces be- tween 320 and 100 yards ranges, ten rounds in all, , with sights fixed at 200 yards, and fixed bayonets. I The idea of the last practice is to train soldiers to fire effectively on an advancing enemy when there is no time to adjust their back-sights. By combining these three stages, the prizes can only, be secured by really good all-round Volunteers, instead of being won by what are I known in the force as "pot-hunters," men who remain in the force and practice shooting with all sorts of artificial aids, for the sole purpose of making money by obtaining prizes, and who are, therefore, no soldiers, but often take benefits which ought togo to more deserv- ing men. A fair number of the members of the com- pany, including Captain Buckton and 'Lieutenant Appleton, attended and fired on Saturday, the chief scores being as follows :-- • let 2nd 3rd stage. stage. stage. Total. 1. Col.-Sergt. Jolley 30 53 18 101 2. Sergeant Spencer 2B 55 15 98 3. Private Plinston 4. Sergeant Taylor , 35 42 15 92 1 Bugle-Major Plinston 22 51 9 82 A Captain Buckton 2l 43 18 82 6. Corporal Russell 7. Private Davies The result of the competition was an open question until the last shot was fired, so that Col.-Sergeant Jolley may well be congratulated on being the holder of the cup for the year. The first five men are, of course, the win- ners of the money prizes.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: DIE SHIP CANAL AND DRUNKENNESS.

The quarterly meeting of the Standing Joint Com- mittee of Cheshire was held at Cheshire Castle on Satur- day. A letter was read from the Home Secretary sanctioning an increase in the county police force to the extent of 20 constables and four sergeants. The Chief Constable(Col. Hamersley)presented his quarterly report, giving a total of 3,298 persons apprehended and sum- awned (an increase of 725 compared with the correspond- ing quarter of last year), 43 committed for trial, 2,898 summarily convicted, and 357 discharged. The increase was attributable to proceedings under the dog muzzling order. During the year ended March 31, 58,793 vagrants had been relieved in the various unions throughout the county, or a decrease of 5,927 compared with the previous year, and an increase of 2,279 over 1885. The Altrincham and Nantwich Unions showed an increase in the number of vagrants relieved over 1889 of 56 and 243 respectively, while the decrease in the Wirral and Birkenhead Unions was 1,659 and 1,070 respectively. During the quarter ended the 31st May last, 770 males and 125 females were proceeded against for drunkenness, and 693 males and 142 females in the same period of last year, representing an increase of 77 males and a decrease ot 17 females, or in comparison with the corresponding quarter of 1885, an increase of 175 males and 55 females. Twenty-eight licensed houses had been proceeded against during the year, resulting in 13 convictions and 15 discharged. Two hundred and fifteen members of the force now held the St. John's Ambulance certificate of proficiency. Mr. M. T. Graveson (Liscard) called attention to the increase of drunkenness disclosed in the report. He thought the standing joint committee ought to look into thismatter more diligently than they did, and he feared there was not that earnestness on the part of the police in dealing with drunkenness that there might be. He believed if the law were put in operation they should see a considerable diminution of this crime of drunkenness. He suggested that in case of festivals, holidays, sports, &c., placards might be posted warning the public that a special look-out would be kept by the police for cases of drunkenness.—The Chairman reminded Mr. Graveson that the population of the county was increasing largely, and said there was also the large floating population in- troduced by the Ship Canal Works to be taken into consideration.—Mr. James Smith (New Brighton) point- ed out that the figures in the report showed an immedi- ate increase in the last few months. (Hear, hear.)— Mr, James Tomkinson also remarked that, although the population had increased, the percentage of drunkenness to population was out of all proportion compared with 1885. There was an increase of 22 per cent, in the case of males, and of 40 per cent. in the case of females.— Mr. Lister thought that was accounted for in a great measure by the Ship Canal. He believed the police al- ready interfered sufficiently with the liberty of the subject.—Mr. R. Howard (a magistr4e) thought the police should exercise greater surveillance over public houses.—The Chief Constable contended that the police were already doing their duty, and if they did any more they would be interfering with the liberty of the sub- ject unduly. He pointed out the difficulty of obtaining convictions against publicans.—lt was ultimately re- solved that the Chief Constable should be empowered to obtain legal assistance in all cases against licensed victuallers. It may be that there are some additions to the thirsty section of the population among the employes on the Manchester Ship Canal, but it is pleasant to bear witness that as a rule the navvies are an orderly body of men, and the manner in which they are looked after morally, intellectually, and spiritually is one of the remarkable features of the singularly good relations maintained between them and the contractors.

Warrington.,22aLl July, 1890. THE DEATH OP ELMO. Sir,—Bung is dead. He has been .an ,tritfortunate bantling, and is declared illegitimate. flerwo-s brought into existence over. two years ago, bubeing such an ill- favoured brat, there was not a town 'in:England would give him room. 'Warrington would mothave him, and all the other towns followed suit. 'He wags kept in concealment, at Arytnurse, for twe'years,' but. rfinding a new foster father ditthe name of 05h ,being a ' rather headstrong Sallow, thought he wontd—isaving, as he believed, a fair excuse—try to rush 'him for main- tenance on the community. But it wasno go. :He was rejected for his ugliness two years ago,and whembrought forward again he was found to be more ill-favoured and mischevious than formerly, so that Isis 'foster father was compelled to abandon him, and let him perish of sheer inanition. But he hasttwo relatives who-survive. Slot strong enough to stand the work of the.surnmex;.they are to go to the seaside until November, -whenethey , expect that the rest and pure air will so Saretretigtbsn , them that they may ps,se through and auriive albtice winter storm. Some people say they will have to.uridek- , go surgical operations at the hands of cloctors•freinuthe Unionist College. Be that as it may,it behoves,us—yen, f sir—and I and others—to watch their mervemenM. Their ' ~names are Bill Tithe—a very mischevions fellow, fond , grabbing that which 'does not belong to him on irpea thatr his pious ancester left it him; wholhat pious. ancestor was many people would like to 'know. The sgher is ) Bill Land-purchase in Ireland—a long imam., m one Bill robs the Nonconformist, and gwivesithe pro- -ceeds to what is called the church. The other robs the , Sriglish taxpayer to enrich the wealthy Iris% landowner; Also poor Irish landowners and the poor Irish 'tenant are deft out in the cold. These two robbers must 'hem-un- ix:illy met, and in the interval from now to November let. their characters be exposed to the tisiblic gaze. 'Tithe is doomed; he may bephysicked and nursed., And have the benefit of the opinions and surgical skill of,. all theftate Doctors, including Heatington and Clesmberlain, down to Sir Joseph Bailey and Byron Reed, but it will be .only, a lingering consumption. He is suffering trans 4rgan:c decay in a vital part, and if we live till Christmas weshall see what will become of Tithe and Irish Land- Purchase. They are sure of a rasping in the House of Conuricns, but they have friends and soothing syrup lin' " the other place." There will be a chance of rooting -the Radicalism of the Unionists on these subjects. They .are not dead yet, Tithe and Irish Land-Purchase, and shotild they die they will not, like Bung, leave a large amount ' of wealth behind for numerous claimants to wrangle', over. ,Ilung leaves £350,000 in •hscrd cash of intestate, property, and a host of claimants have sprung up as heirs-attlaw to divide the wealth. Welshmen claim a slice for intermediate and higher education. I hope they; may get it. Wales is poor in endowments, and what few there arelmve most of them been scandalously mis- managed. £350,000 in hard cash is .a large sum. Could not a few'thousands, say £5,000, he divided or invested among those old soldiers who are workimusod, some of them, and.others are worse off —sliding.down the path of penury andrwant to a pauper's grave. Were it not for the patriotio.and benevolent feeling ot individual, some of these old men must have starved for want of the common necessaries of life. I care but little, personally, ,how Bung's money may go, the bulk of it, but it would rojoice my beast to know that the modest sum I have named had gone to cheer the hearts of the brave men who stood without flinching between our -country and her foes, in the face of death, on the battlefietd.—l am, Sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges,:Zuly 21st, 1890.

They were engaged on the scaffold at the lock which is in course of construction at Weston Point, when one of the planks on the gantrey slipped, and they were thrown into the base of the lock. Fortunately, they were not seriously iniored, and escaped with a . .. ,_

shiack to the system. SHIP CANAL FATALITY. George Humphries, 55 years of age, employed as a road cleaner on the Acton Grange Section of the Ship Canal met with a fatal accident on Wednesday afternoon. The deceased, who went by the name of " Darkie " amongst his fellow-workmen„ was engaged near a coal store in cleaning the line when he was knocked down and run over by two trucks which were being pushed along by an engine. The body was shockingly mutilated, and death was instantaneous. The body was removed to the Ship Canal Hospital at Thelwall, pending the inquest. The deceased, it is said, was hard of hearing. ..EXTRAORDINARY sBUTRAGE AT EASTHAM. On Sunday a party of visitors to Eastham were an- noyed by comments passed on them by a number of Ship Canal navvies, and the men of the party at last took objection to some of the Temarks. They were then set upon by the navvies, and one of them, a young man maned James Lovell, was knocked over the embankment on to the shore. He was-so seriously injured that his removal to the Birkenhead Borough Hospital was neces- sary, and three of the cam, named respectively Peddie, Philbin and Dawson, were taken into custody on a charge

of assault. At Birkenhead, on 'Thursday, a ship Canal borer named John Simons, was charged in custody, with as- saulting a Liverpool pilot named Wm. Hughes, near Easthatn, on Alonday. Superintendent Hindley said the Canal navvies -were becoming so riotous and using such disgraceful language that the police could not cope with them. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sent to goal for three months, with hard labour.

RUNCORN DISTRICT. Operations are progressing favourably on this sect ion So far as the otlserseetions are concerned, however great the engineering difficulties may be, they are compara- tively insignificant as-oompared with those which must necessarily be encountered in the neighbourhood of Run- corn where a long length of river bed has to be dealt with, to furnish a walhwhich will separate the natural course of the stream from the intended watercourse to Manchester. For some time past the operations have been somewhat hampered, the difficulties to be met being apparently somewhat greater than was at first surmised, owing to the peculiar formation of the bed of the river. Within an exceedingly short distance from a splendid foundation 'óf rock, a deep bed of running sand has had to be encountered, and a vast amount of en- gineering skill has' hatito be brought to bear to surmount the difficulty. At the present time satisfactory pro- gress is being made at the Old Quay, also near Runcorn Bridge, and lower down the river, in the directioa of , Weston Point. A long length of wall has been erected at the Old Quay, thelaack is in an advanced stage of progress, whilst the-sea wall from" No Man's Land," in the direction of Messrs': Wigg Bros. and Steele's, is gradu- ally beingexterided. 'An interesting piece of work is being watched moat, attentively nearly opposite Old Bridgewater House. In the river has been formed a bed, which will, doubtless, be encased in stone, so as to form the permanent river-wall. Lower down the stream an- other lock is in process of formation. On Frodsham Score the work is progressing most favourably. VISIT OF STEAMSHIP OWNERS. The Ship Canal avotks were inspected on Wednes- day, by representatives of a number of steam- ship owners who are engaged in the Continental trade. The party comprised the following firms, or their representatives :—Messrs. , Bailey and Leetham, Hull, trading with tihe Baltic ports; Messrs. Bahr, Behrend, and Ross,'Llyerpool, trading with the Spanish and Baltic ports Co-operative Wholesale Society, Man- chester, trading With 'Hamburg, Rouen, and Calais; Messrs. Crosby, Kerr and Co., Liverpool ; Messrs. Donald Come and Co., Liverpool; the General Steam Naviga- tion Company, London--and Mr. George Simpson, Man- chester agent Messrs.crohn Good and Sons, Hull ; the Goole Steamship Company, trading with Antwerp, Rotterdam, and Ghent'; = Mr. J. C. Harker, representing a French company; Messrs. J. and P. Hutchinson, Glas- gow, trading with Rouen, Nantes, and Havre ; the Hum- ber Steamship Company, Goole, trading with Ghent, Rouen, and Jersey ; Mr:FeterM'Guffin, Liverpool—Baltic trade ; Messrs. Macwatty and Co., Liverpool—Mediter- ranean trade; Messrs. Morley, Clark, and Co., Hull— Baltic trade; Messrs. Papayanni and Co.; Liverpool— Mediterranean trade; Messrs. H. G. Perlbach and Co., London—Baltic trade:: Messrs. Wilson, Sons, and Co., Hull, and Messrs. Grandchamp and Sons, Rouen; Messrs. J. D. Heviitt and Co., London.' The m Ship Canal Company we represented by Mr. Alder- man W. H. Bailey, one of the directors, and Mr. Marshall Stevens, who-very courteously acted as cicerones to the party. The visitors assembled at the Manchester end of the canal, and were conveyed by rail along the banks of the great waterway to Runcorn. There a halt was made for luncheon, which was served in Bridgewater House. From this point-tor'Eastham the party were con- veyed by steamer. Verylceen interest was manifested in the undertaking, andparticularly in the arrangements for diverting important lines of railway and for provid- ing the great lacks. When-the visitors had assembled in the hotel at Eastham, Mr. stVestray proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Bailey, as representing the Ship Canal Company, for the courtesy that had been extended to them. He had, he said, been perfectly astounded at the magnitude of the operations. and was very grateful for the opportunity he had had of seeing them in pro- gress.—Mr. Joseph Good, as a- representative of the east coast trade, seconded the raetien.—Major Clarke (Messrs. Morley, Clarke and Co.) said 'he did not think they should look upon the Manchester Ship Canal as in any way, opposed to those who traded With the Continent from the ports on the East coast. He hoped there would be enough trade for all of them., and that the promoters of the canal would be amply remunerated for their great outlay. The work had been cartied on with marvellous rapidity ; he was amazed to rase much had been done in so short a time..—Mr. Taylor.'('Messrs. Papayanni and Co., Liverpool), said what was good for Manchester would be good for the country, =id fc.r our own county in particular.—Mr. Harrison -(Lisarrpool) put the resolu- tion to the meeting, and it was adopted with acclama- ' tion.—Mr. Alderman Bailey said he regarded this as one re the most influential cleputationstbat had ever visited the canal, seeing they were so largely engaged in the steamship trade between England rand the Continent, and knew the importance of economy of force inconnec- Alen with such work. As they well inew, a ton of goods WIL 3 like water goingdown a hill. If it had to be sent from one part of the world to another it was like water--it took the line cf least resistance,—and he believed that in the Ship Canal they had that line between Manchester and foreign ports, and if they could take a ton of goods from any part, from the vineyz.rds, gardens, quarries or mines of any country, -right on to Manchester, they would not stay to land that ton of goods anywhere en route if it could be demonstrated that it would cost more money to send -it a part of the journey by rail. Az to Liverpool he be- lieved the thirty-three miles between it and Manchester .wouldbe the busiest spot on the face of the earth. It was impossible to do good to Manchester without doing good to liverpool, and any points touching division of cargo or port of call would be soon arranged, and in a way that would reflect credit on all persons concerned. Little conflicting interests would be smoothed down and when the Canal was finished they would, be anticipated, all task in tile sunshine of prosperity. They were en- gaged in an enterprise that would, they believed, not only redound,to their own individual profit, bat increase the wealth of one of the busiest centres on the face of the globe. (Applause.) The party then proeeeded to Liverpool, and there separated.

SUDDEN DEATHS AT WARRINGTON.

Joseph Hall, 50 years of age, a foTehand puddler at the works of Messrs. Monks, hail, and Co., and residing at 62, Catherine-St., died suddenly on Fri- , day morning. He appeared to be in his usual ' health on Thursday night, and after retiring to bed ' about nine o'clock, got qo to go to his work at five o'clock. He left the heuse without complaining, and worked for about twenty minutes, when he sat down near his furnace and said to a young man working close by, " I feel very ill." He shortly afterwards fell forward, and Dr. Brooks was imme- diately sent for. On the arrival of that gentleman be pronounced life to be extinct. henry Bithell, 60 wars of age, a chimney sweep, living at 83, Mersey-st.. was foinad dead about eleven nlelock on Thursday night. It is stated that the deeeased had been drinking heavily lota few weeks I past, and was under the influence of drink on Thursday night. About half-past saix o'clock he fell •and out hi a eyebrow, and his wife assisted hi en to the sofa. She left the house until about eleven o'clock and when she returned she found him dead. His body was then lying ou the sofa.

ACCIDENT TO A lI.Asii:ENDER ON THE PENICETIT 'Bus. An accident occurred on Saturday night, as the 10 o'clock 'bus was running from Warrington to Penketh. Whemit arrived off the end of Heath- road, it stopped, as is .customary, to allow pas- sengers to alight. One man, named Goulding, who was coming .down from the, top of the 'bus, slipped while on the steps and felt heavily to the ground. He was picked up,and carried to his home, which is ' close by. Dr. Murray.was sent for, and upon exam- ination it was found that Goulding had received a severe gash at the back of ice head,two inches long, which laid the hone bare, besides a severe shaking. The wound was dressed and bound, and up to the present it is progressing farourably. Goulding's son had his arm 43roken in tie machinery at the Sankey Wire MilLsa week or two back. fr2entrruALit4:st. On Monday evening a meeting was held at the British IVorlimen, iforsemarket-st., arranged by .a few persons interested in the,inyestigation of spiri- tualism. Mrs. Green, of Ileywood, trance speaker and clairvoyant, gave an address on "The power of spirit over matter," and at .the,clese of the address gave a number of clairvoyant desoriptions of friends departed, many of whom were recognized, but not all. In one case, the medium described a man whom she believed to be sanative, though living at a con- siderabledistance from Warrington, and said the per- son with whom he appeared to be connected would shortly hear from him. Whenasked howshe accounted for this psychological phenomenon,- she acknow- lodged that it was a mystery to herself, but fre- quently occurred. Mr. W. PAUL'S GIRLS' FRIF.WDLY SOCIETY. On Saturday the members of the St. Paul's branch of the Girls' Friendly Society celebrated their annual festival. Wilkinson (vicar), and T. Emnaott (curate), I. Philips (Orford), and a few friends, left the Central Station for Southport. On arriving there, the party proceeded to St. Andrew's Church, where a short service was held, and an address delivered to the girls by the Rev. Canon Cross, D.D. All then dispersed to enjoy themselves in the town, and met again at five o'clock for tea. The Vicar,address- ing the girls, begged them to endeavour to live up to the high standard of the society. div.head: DROWNING CASE AT WALT.
div.p: DROWNING CASE AT WALT.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. Worsiey, coroner,,held an inquest at Lower Walton, with regard to rthe death of ahoy named Joseph Dawson, who lived with his parents at , Lower Walton. and who was drowned nythe canal at Walton, on Sunday after- noon. 'Thedeceased, who was ten years of age, was playing with some companions near to the swing bridge, about midway between Tom Paine's itridP and Walton Arches. They had constructed a matt, and as the oanal is almost filled in, they did mot seem to realise their perilous position. •The de-) ceased over-,balanced himself and fell into the water, and before he Gould be rescued was drowned. The body was recovered in about an hour afterwards. The verdict of, the jury was to the effect that the deceased was accidentally drowned. TRIEERRANCR WORK IN THIS OPEN-AIR. _

On Sunday the meetings of the Workingmen's Open-air Totnl Abstinence Mission were held as usual on he ,enclosed ground off Bewsey-st. /At the afternoon "meeting Mr. Beswick was in 'the chair, and gave .a speech upon the evils resulting from intemperance. Messrs. C. If. Mills and J. O'Reilly also addressed the Meeting. At the ,even- ing meeting Mr. T. Frain presided, and was sup-' ported ky Messrs. J. Leicester, E.,Robertson, J.' Baker, CAL Mills; J. O'Reilly, G. Wild, and g. Price, all of whom gave addresses. Mr. T. Marshall con- ducted tbe singing. The meeting was brought to ,a close by Mr. E. *Robertson singing "God be with' you till we meet again." The work of the mission has been very Isuecessful, and the meetings have been well attended. Many total abstinence pledges have been taken.
WARRENGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB BUILDIIO6 iCOMPANY, LIMITED. . I

This Company report that they have not thought it necessary to issue any fresh shares during the, past year, as it is, considered that the shares already taken up will fully cover the costs of the under- taking so far es at present determined upon. The profit and loss account shows an available balance of £230 12s. 7d. Thedirectors recommend a pay- ment of a dividend the same as last year, viz., after the rate of three per cent. per annum. This will absorb about ...,,e204 l7s. which will leave about, .£25 15s. 7d. to go in reduction of the preliminary; expenses account, the balance of which, yet to be; paid out of profits, .3vill amount to £32 lfis. 11d. ' The directors who retire by rotation at this time are Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., John White, Esq., J.P., Alderman.:John E. Wright, Messrs. Robert Isherwood, and William Dickens. They are eligible for re-election. The directors again urge upon each shareholder the desirability of using his best endeavotirs according to his opportunity, to induce Conservatives residing or having business in the borough to become members of the club, and thus serve the interests of the club, the Conservative cause, and of the company. ST. MARY'S CHURCH, GREAT SANKEY. The parOchial trip in connection with St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, took place on Monday, Southport being the chosen destination. At 925 a.m, a special train containing 250 of the parishion- ers of Sankey and Peoketh left Sankey Station, and Southport was reached at 10.10 a.m. On arrival , there the whole party dispersed,,and sought enjoy- ment in various directions. Amongst the places visited were the Churchtown Botanical Gardens ; and ferneries, the Winter Gardens, &c. Some of the party went to the sands, and others took steamer and sailed to Blackpool and back. The teachers and the members of the San- key and Penketh choirs had dinner and tea at the Royal Hotel. The Vicar (the Rev. E. S. Jackson), the curate (the Rev. T. E. Winder), the church- wardens and choirmasters, accompanied the party. A pleasing feature of the excursion was the taking of the Conservative widows, 34 in number, of Sankey and Penketh, free of expense. Mr. P. Pown- all, with whom the idea originated, collected money to defray the expense, and under his leadership an enjoyable day was spent. They were provided with a knife-and-fork tea at the Searisbriek Hotel. The return train left Southport at 9.10 p.m., and reached Sankey about 10.11. TRE WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOMETY. Mr. Thos. Birchall, president, occupied the chair at the quaiterly meeting of the Warrington Indus- trial Co-operative Society, which was held in the Sankey-st. Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening. IThe 118th quarterly report wae submitted to the I meeting, and was approved on the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. John Newell. It .stated that the sales for the quarter had been 17,81035. Bd., and that the profits, after meeting all liabilities, allowing for fixed stock, &c., would allow of a dividend of 3s. 2d. in the .E on the pur- chases of members. The Chairman congratulated the-meeting upon the satisfactory report which the Committee had been able to present. It was true therehad been a little diminution in the sales, but I the Mkt quarter was what was generally known as; the slack quarter. At the same time, it, was pleas-1 ing .to know that the dividend had not been affected. The Managing Secretary (Mr. A. IL Rathbone.) read the minutes of the various Com- mittee meetings. At one meeting a letter was read fromthe ms.nagers of the People's College. It stated that the necessity for good cooking was felt in con- nection with the early training of the working class children, and that it was most desirable that cook- ing classes should be organized in connection with the College. To provide for that object it was neces- sary to raise funds for the erection of a class-room. The Committee of the Co-operative Society consid- ered that a class of the description referred to would he of considerable advantage to the female portion of the scholars, and recommended that a donation of SO be granted. The Chairman, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, remarked that the Society to some extent was an educational institu- tion, and the Committee considered that .£5 taken out of their educational fund would be very well spent for the purpose named. The society did credit to itself by subscribing to such a worthy object. (Hear, hear.) Mr. John Newell seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried.

- MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—COUOII advices from New York report a fluctuating market yesterday, and a num- ber of conflicting circumstances are mentioned in explanation of this, In the first Instance, favourable advices from Liver- pool appear to have imparted some buoyancy to the situation. Although the sales of cotton in Liverpool are large, amoanting to 12,000 bales, and this following upon 17,003 bales sold yesterday, the actual values there are no dearer; indeed, futures are said to be in some positions fractionally lower. Still, the general tone of affairs is firm, and full prices are asked in all directions. There is not much alteration as to the condition of the principal markets, but if anything it would ; appear almost as if the demand for the better makes of shirt- lugs ancbsheetings to which we have referred frequently of late is now for the time satisfied, LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY.—StIgRT : A. fair to good demand for pieces at steady rates ; other refined goods un- altered ; beet a steadier tendency; July-August buyers 13s 6d and sellers 13s 8d to 13s 94 ; November sold at 12s 3d •, cane a steady sale. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, PRIDAY.—Beef meets a moder- ate request at ' the lately reduced rates. In Pork a firmer feeling is experienced. YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Royal assent was given by Com- mission to 62 public and private Bills, including the Consolidated fund No. 2, Green Spaces, Working Classes Dwellings, Education Code, Deeds of Arrangement in Land, Revenue regulations, Western Australian Con- stitution, and Colonial Courts of Admiralty. The Lord Chancellor, Earl Coventry, and Earl Limerick, were the Lord Commissioners. Several provisional orders ad- vanced a stage. THE GUARDS.—Lord Sandhurst drew attention to the recent occurrences in connection with the 2nd Battalion Grenadier Guards, and moved for papers.—The Duke of Cambridge deprecated discussion on the subject, and said discipline in the army could not be preserved if such a discussion took place. Earl Brownlow expressed similar views, and said that papers could not be laid on the table with duo regard to public interests. The motion was then withdrawn.—The remaining Orders were disposed of, and the House adjourned at 6.30. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Tim CLYDE NAVIGATION BILL.—One hour and a half was consumed in the consideration of the Clyde Navigation Bill, Which was eventually read a third time. PREMIUMS FOR HORSE BEREDING.—MT. CHAPLIN, in reply to Mr. Alfred Pease, said he should personally be glad to see the £5,000 now given for the Queen's premiums, and the encouragement of horse breeding, raised to £lo,ooo,but the question was one for the treasury to consider. THE POTATO BLIGHT.—Mr. BALFOUR, replying to Messrs. Glynn and Sexton, said the Government were carefully watching the reports of the potatoblight on the Irish sea- board. He had no present reaion to anticipate the neces- sity of relaxing the rules respecting out door relief. LIGHT Crotn.—Mr. GOSCHEN inhormed Sir W. Harcourt that seeing the state of public business he should not press the Bill to further call in light gold. He hoped, however, to deal with the subject before the and of the financial year. THE GRENADIER GUARDS. --Mr. STANHOPE Informed Mr. Conybeare that he did not see that any useful pur- pose would be served by laying before Parliament de- faulter sheets of the men of the 2nd Battalion Grenadier Guards who had been sentenced to imprisonment.—Mr. GRAHAM asked if the men had not borne good conduct records, and said any such circumstances had no doubt been taken into consideration by the Court Martial (oh.) Ms. STANHOPE, replying to Mr. Conybeare,said that after writing to the:newspapers saying he had not resigned, Col. Maitland reconsidered his determination and un- reservedly resigned the command of the Grenadier Guards. His resignation had been accepted, and he had been placed on half pay. JUSTICE HARRISON'S CHARGE :—Mr. BALFOUR. replving Mr. Dillon, said from a private letter from Justice Harrison, relative to the recent charge to the Grend Jury at Galway, he found the charge was not com- mitted to writing, and that he had official documents 'before him that a great many outrages had been com- mitted at the East Riding in respect of none of which had any person been made amenable. rLEFT SITTING.]

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
- - ANOTHER GRENADIER SENTENCED. The sixth man of the Grenadiers tried by court. martial has been sentenced to two years' imprisonment.
DROWNED WHILE BATHING. This morning, Corporal Taylor, of the Royal Irish Fusiliers,was drowned while bathing in the River Shannon at Athlone.
GENERAL LORD WOLSELEY IN IRELAND. General Lord Wolseley arrived in Dublin yesterday, to take up his new dutka as commander of the forces in Ireland.
YESTERDAY'S CRICKET. The Lancashire second in,nings closed for 237 yester- day. Sussex first innings closed for 91; second innings two for 35. Middlesex, six for 121. AN APPOINTMENT.

The Queen haii--;p;i:OvWC iice—aim- ointment of Sir Michael Henry Gallway, Attorney General of Natal, as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the colony. THE THREATENED SEAMEN'S STRIKE. A Newcastle correspondent says that, in consequence of the threatened strike of British seamen, foreign sea- men are being engaged for British steamers at the North- ern ports, and in some cases at lower wages.

POISIONED By WINKLES. A family named Cross, residing at Clapton-park, London, are alleged to have been poisoned through eat- ing winkles. The father succumbed on Wednesday night, but the other members of the family recovered, after suffering great pain. DIFFICULTIES AT TEE LONDON DOCKS.

The arrangements entered into on Thursday between the London and St. Katharine's Docks Company and the Dock Labourers' Union, whereby Union tickets might be examined inside the docks, was, after a slight hitch, carried out yesterday morning, and work was resumed.

div.head: BISLEY MEETING.
div.p: THE BISLEY MEETING.

Yesterday the Wantage Prize of £ll was won by Lieut. Carpenter, of the Hon. Artillery Company ; and the Rapid Prize has been gained by Sergt. T. Manghan, Royal Marine L. I. The winners of the Robin Hood Prize are Private Mac Kay, Dumbarton, and Sergeant Baird, Lanark. The Dudley Prize has been won by Captain Fremantle, Ist Beds. with 46 points. The match between the London Rifle Brigade and the Cape team, seven shots at three distances, ten men a-side, resulted in favour of London by one point (873 to 672). The Cape team had to strike 86 points from their score, owing to a light-pull trigger. THE TRAGIC AFFAIR AT CREWE. SENSATIONAL DEVELOPMENT. ,

At Crewe vesterday, Charles Lowndes, foreman, was ebarged with attempting to murder Arthur Townley, his brother-in-law. Townley had his face, nose, and ears crossed with bandages., He said en Sunday night he went to the house of his father-in-law, John Platt. When he got inside the kitchen the prisoner struck at him and his father-in-law hit him two violent blows in the mouth. He retreated towards the door, when Lowndes followed him, tripped him on his back, and stabbed him in the face, throat, and neck. Lowndes said he had waited for an opportunity to cut his throat. He thought both Lowndes and Platt had deliberately planned to kill him. At this point Supt. Leah applied for the arrest of Platt, who was in court as a witness for the defence. Platt was immediately arrested and placed alongside Lowndes in the dock. Both prisoners were remanded.

THE DUNLO DIVORCE CASE. The hearing of the Dunlo divorce case was resumed on Friday morning. Charles Dunn, who had been coach- man to Mr. Wertheimer, was cross-examined. Ile never saw any familiarity between Lady Dunlo and Mr. Wer- theimer after her marriage. Mr. Marmaduke Wood, officer in the Somersetshire Militia, said he asked Lady Dunk, at the last Brighton Races why she went about with Wertheimer, and she said she was devoted to him. —Cross-examined: The witness admitted stating at the Lyric Club on Thursday night that Lord Albert Osborne and Lord Dunlo tossed up for Lady Dunlo, and that Lord Dunlo was successful. Mr. Lockwood opened the case for Lady Dunlo, and declared that although she fell a victim to Weston, she was not the mistress of Werthei- mer, although he was deeply aeached to her and wished her to marry hirn.

div.head: SIR GILBERT GREENALL AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SIR GILBERT GREENALL AT ST. HELENS.

Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P. for Warring- ton, laid the memorial stone of a new chancel in connection with St. Thomas's Church, West- .field-street, St. Helens, on Thursday. The church was erected in 1838-9 at a cost of between £5,000 and £6;000 by Mr. Peter Greenall, the elder brother of Sir Gilbert. In November, 1888, at was decided to make the church free and open, and this movement was succeeded by the present one forereeting a new chancel, small chapel for vestry meetings, Aim, organ chamber, and clergy and choir vestries, at an estimated cost of about £2,800. -Sir Gilbert Greenall was waited upon by the vicar, the Rey.. j. C. Pigot, M.A., who is a grand- -son of the late Mrs. Peter Greenall, and the hon. gentleman promised £lOOO towards the fund. Messrs. Pilkington Brothers also promised £250 and Colonel Gamble, C.D., Mr. W. Pilkington, D.L., Mr. Thomas Pilkington, and Mr. J. Robinson £lOO ,each. The contract was let to Messrs. Bothwell and Sons, who are using the best Ruabou terra-cotta bricks to face both inside and out, and who will re- • .seat the body of the church and lower the gallery frotit. The whole is to be completed by March next. The building will then be about thirty feet longer And will accommodate 800 worshippers. ' There was a very large attendance at the ceremoity on Thursday afternoon. Among those present, in addition to Sir Gilbert, were Lady Greenall, the Misses Greene'', , Miss Bishop, Mrs. 11 Gamble, Mrs. FL S. Hall, Alderman J. Harrison, the Revs_ J. C. Pigot (vicar), H. S. Bolton, M. F. Binney, 3. L. Saywell, H. Mitchell, H. A. Arnold, G. Lakeman. 'l'. J. Powell, J. Pullebank, and J. F. H. Parker. After devotional exercises, cbnducted by the Vicar,the latter handed to Sir Gilbert Greenall a splendid ivory handled silver, trowel, on the front of which was an engraved design of the new chancel. On the reverse side appeared the inscription "Presented to Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., on the occasion of his laying the memorial stone of the church of St. Thomas's, Eccles- ton., as an acknowledgment of his very generous , assistance. Eve of St. James 1890." Sir Gilbert Greenall then formally laid the stone, after which i he gave a brief address, n the course of which be ex- • pressed the pleasure it afforded him to be present, and said it was always, of course, of very great satisfaction to him to be associated with any good work. He inti- mated that his son had instructed him to offer a dona- tion of £5O, and his daughters £25 each. He hoped Gred's blessing would rest upon the work they had begun that day.—The Rev. J. C. Pigott (vicar) also spoke, and remarking that the parishioners vere under a very great debt of gratitude to Sir Gilbert, said that in addi- tion to the £l,OOO promised by Sir Gilbert Greenall, , Lady Greenall had kindly promised £5OO on her own behalf. (Applause.)—The proceedings then terminated with the singing of a hymn and prayer.

Sr. JAMES'S, LATCHFORD. The dedication festival in connection with St. James's Church, Latchford, took place yesterdar: The services commenced with the celebration or the Holy Communion at 8 a.m. and Matins half-11.1)- hour later. There was a fair congregation. and tbir service was conducted by the Vicar, the 80. Slater. In the evening there was festal evensong. n The body of the church was well filled, and the co- gregation listened with evident interest to a ser'" mon by the Lord Bishop of Chester. The lessons and prayers were read by the Vicar. The offertories were in aid of the church expenses: The altar, font, and chancel screens had been decked with flowerer. principally lilies, for the occasion. A feature of the decorations was a handsome cress of white' lilies on the altar. The service was of a choral, charactertand Mr. F. Booth presided at the organ.. Total B4l Total 67 A FATAL FALL AT DOUGLAS.

An inquest was held at Douglas, on Saturday, as to the death of Alfred Endall, upwards of 10 years of age, traveller for the North 13ritish Rubber Co., and who resided at Rock Ferry. Deceased, who had many friends in Warrington, which town he had visited on business for many years, arrived at Douglas on the previous Monday on business for the firm, and put up at the Regent Hotel, where he usually stayed. On Friday he returned to the hotel shortly before eleven o'clock. He went into the smokeroom, had a glass of brandy, and. went up- stairs to go to his bedrooms a few minutes past eleven. The waiter spoke to him at the foot of the , stairs, asking him what time he intended to cross to Liverpool next day, and deceased to all appear- ances was sober. A minpte or two *afterwards the. waiter heard a heavy fall, and on running to the stairs found the deceased lying on the stairs, head downwards, bleeding from the nose and ears. lie was remnved to the smokeroom, but he never re- covered consciousness, dying about five o'clock the following morning. At the inquest Dr. Black said the immediate cause of death was compression of the brain, and suggested that deceased might have fallen in a fit. The jury returned a verdict of "Ac- cidental death." WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT. A sitting of this Court was held on. Thins-day, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The cause list comprised 5 default summonses. 2 adjourned plaints, 133 original plaints, and 43 original judgment surn7 monses.—Mr. Hatton (from the office of Messrs. Robert Davies, Sharp, anti Kirkconnell) applied for the discharge of James Moss, a debtor, who had carried on business as a quarry proprietor at Helsby. Mr. Hatton explained that the debtor's affairs had beed liquidated by arrangement, and he applied, under the Discharge and Closure Act, 1887, for his discharge. The trustee, in answer to his Honour, said he had no objection to make to the application, and his Honour made an order for the discharge.— Thomas Dutton, a wheelwright, living at Burton- I wood, sued Messrs. Skelton, ironmongers, Horse- market-St., for 10,s. 6d., the cost of three journeys to Warringion. On the 12th May the plaintiff bought- some barbed wire for fencing from the defendants and paid for it. The cost was 16s. 6d. He subse- quently, it was alieged, sent a man for the wire. but the defendants would not part with it. He also sent on two subsequent occasions for it, and he now claimed 10s. 6c1., the cost of the journeys to War- rington. The defence was that the wire had not been sent for and his Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for theamount claimed.
